theory_units.title: Create Audience Presence with Subjective Framing
theory_units.summary: Position the camera at eye-level and up close to the subject to make the viewer feel 'within' the scene, transforming observed action into an experienced reality.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to draw the audience deeply into the character's perspective or the immediate action, making them feel like participants rather than mere observers.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience experiences a stronger sense of 'presence,' feeling included in the pictorial space as if it were real three-dimensional space, and perceives subjects as life-sized and immediate.
theory_units.caution: Can limit wider context if used exclusively; balance with establishing shots when necessary.

theory_units.title: Preserve Illusion in Continuity Style
theory_units.summary: Avoid techniques that draw attention to the filmmaking process itself to ensure the audience remains immersed in the story's illusion.
theory_units.applies_when: Adhering to the principles of the classical Hollywood 'continuity style.'
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamless storytelling that keeps the audience focused on the narrative and characters without being reminded they are watching a film.
theory_units.caution: Intentionally breaking this rule can be used for avant-garde or experimental effects, but will disrupt the continuity style's intended immersion.

theory_units.title: Choose Pacing via Long Take or Fast Cutting
theory_units.summary: Directors must decide between staging action within a single long sequence shot or using fast cutting to control the scene's rhythm and impact.
theory_units.applies_when: When deciding the rhythm and visual presentation of a specific action sequence or narrative beat.
theory_units.expected_effect: A long sequence shot can build tension, create realism, and emphasize continuous time/space, while fast cutting can accelerate pacing, intensify action, and fragment perception.
theory_units.caution: A poorly executed long take can feel slow or unmotivated; excessive fast cutting can become disorienting or tiring.

theory_units.title: Intentionality in Shot Design
theory_units.summary: The director should actively strive to make every single shot and sequence in the film purposeful and impactful, setting high standards for visual design.
theory_units.applies_when: Throughout the entire filmmaking process, from script to final edit, as a guiding philosophy for all visual and narrative decisions.
theory_units.expected_effect: A highly cohesive, impactful, and visually rich film where no element feels wasted or accidental, contributing meaningfully to the story.
theory_units.caution: Can lead to overthinking or perfectionism, but the core principle is about conscious artistic choices.

theory_units.title: Use Contrasting Visual Elements for Thematic Depth
theory_units.summary: Incorporate visually contrasting background elements with foreground subjects to provide thematic context or underscore historical narratives.
theory_units.applies_when: When a scene's setting or background can offer deeper meaning or historical resonance by contrasting with the immediate foreground action or character.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enriches the scene with symbolic meaning, provides subtext, and visually reinforces narrative themes or historical context without relying solely on dialogue.
theory_units.caution: Overuse can make the symbolism feel heavy-handed; ensure the contrast is relevant and enhances the scene, not distracts from it.

theory_units.title: Pre-visualizing Shots with Camera Angle Projections
theory_units.summary: Utilize camera angle projections to foresight how sets will appear through specific lenses and camera positions, enabling identification of compositional issues, optimization of set construction, and precise planning of camera movements.
theory_units.applies_when: During pre-production, before set construction, when planning shots for complex sets, effects shots (e.g., matte shots, forced perspective), or anticipating camera movements (e.g., panning).
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents costly set modifications, avoids displeasing visual distortion, ensures desired shot composition, optimizes material use, facilitates accurate camera movement planning, and aids in previewing sets for various technical shots.
theory_units.caution: Not using this tool can lead to unforeseen compositional problems and overbuilding. A change in lens or camera position requires a new projection drawing.

theory_units.title: Using Scaled Models for Staging and Camera Setups
theory_units.summary: Employ scaled models as a three-dimensional visualization aid to determine actor staging and camera setups, and to plan logistical movements of cast, crew, and equipment around a set or location.
theory_units.applies_when: During pre-production, particularly for scenes involving complex actor blocking, multiple camera positions, or large numbers of cast/crew.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clarifies and optimizes actor staging and camera setups, improves logistical efficiency for production management.

theory_units.title: Storyboarding for Director Credibility and Pre-planning
theory_units.summary: Directors should extensively storyboard their films to visualize ideas, plan shot flow, and convey an impression of competence and clear pre-planning to the crew, thereby establishing credibility.
theory_units.applies_when: Throughout the pre-production process, especially when a director wants to project authority, ensure efficient communication of vision, and maintain control on set (e.g., when working with a new crew or early in one's career).
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased crew confidence in the director, efficient production process, clear communication of the director's visual intent, and precise execution of the narrative.
theory_units.caution: The myth of 'invented-on-the-set' filmmaking is largely false and can undermine effective pre-planning.

theory_units.title: Storyboard Technique for Pan Shots and Camera Movement
theory_units.summary: When storyboarding scenes with anticipated camera movement, such as pan shots, the artist should first draw the entire scene of action and then indicate the specific framing of the subject within that broader scene.
theory_units.applies_when: Creating storyboards for any scene that involves dynamic camera movement, especially panning or tracking shots, where the camera's path through the environment needs to be clearly illustrated.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a precise and unambiguous visual representation of the camera's movement relative to the overall environment, aiding in accurate execution of complex camera work.
theory_units.caution: Not all storyboard artists employ this method, but it is particularly effective for demonstrating camera movement.

theory_units.title: Leveraging Storyboard Illustrators for Visual Direction
theory_units.summary: Directors who identify a lack of strong visual sense should actively delegate or collaborate with storyboard illustrators to design the shot flow, structuring, staging, and composition of the film.
theory_units.applies_when: A director recognizes a personal limitation in visual conceptualization, or prefers to focus on performance and narrative while entrusting visual design to specialists.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures professional and effective visual structuring, staging, and composition, compensating for the director's visual limitations and leading to a visually coherent film.

theory_units.title: Rigorous Storyboarding for Vision Control (Hitchcock Method)
theory_units.summary: Adopt an elaborate and thorough storyboarding process, as exemplified by Alfred Hitchcock, to precisely refine the director's vision, exert comprehensive control over the entire filmmaking process, and guarantee the exact translation of original creative intentions to the screen.
theory_units.applies_when: A director prioritizes absolute control over the visual outcome, seeks to finalize all creative decisions before shooting commences, and aims for an exact realization of a pre-conceived vision.
theory_units.expected_effect: Unwavering fidelity to the director's original vision, minimal on-set improvisation, a highly predictable and controlled production, and a visually consistent film.
theory_units.caution: This method demands significant upfront time and effort in pre-production.

theory_units.title: Storyboarding for Polished Complex Staging & Kinetic Effects
theory_units.summary: Utilize detailed and comprehensive storyboards as an indispensable tool to achieve 'lapidary polish' and precision in scenes featuring complex staging, intricate blocking, and dynamic (kinetic) visual effects.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning and executing scenes that involve elaborate actor movements, multiple interacting elements, sophisticated camera movements, or significant visual effects that require high precision.
theory_units.expected_effect: Results in highly refined, precise, and visually impactful complex staging and dynamic effects, contributing to a professional and seamless cinematic experience.

theory_units.title: Employ Gothic Lighting for Mood and Set Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Utilize gothic lighting techniques to establish a specific mood and visually enhance the architectural features or general atmosphere of a scene.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming to create a dramatic, mysterious, or somber atmosphere, particularly in settings that benefit from strong contrasts and evocative shadows, such as grand or historical interiors.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a strong sense of drama, mystery, or foreboding; accentuates the visual impact of the setting and its details; reinforces emotional tone.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful control to avoid overly dark or artificial results; ensure lighting choices integrate naturally with the scene's narrative and characters.

theory_units.title: Seamless Composite Crane Shots
theory_units.summary: Execute visually complex, continuous crane shots by combining miniature sets with full-scale sets, using in-camera transitions like dissolves to bridge the shift between environments.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director desires a single, uninterrupted camera movement that traverses different scales or distinct locations (e.g., from exterior rooftop to interior room) within a single shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of grandeur and unbroken perspective, enhancing immersion by eliminating traditional cuts and allowing for a continuous, flowing visual narrative.
theory_units.caution: Demands meticulous pre-planning, precise execution, and careful blending of visual elements (miniatures, full-scale sets, and transitions) to maintain realism and avoid jarring shifts.

theory_units.title: Closer Lens for Action Coverage and Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Obtain supplementary camera coverage of an action or subject by using a closer lens, magnifying details and heightening emotional or narrative importance.
theory_units.applies_when: When an initial wider shot provides context, but a specific action, object, or character's reaction requires greater visual focus, intensity, or detail to be conveyed to the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs the audience's attention to crucial details, intensifies emotional impact, builds tension, or reveals subtle nuances not apparent in a wider shot.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the closer shot adds significant new information or emotional weight; avoid redundant coverage that doesn't advance the narrative or deepen character insight.

theory_units.title: Vertical Pan for Descending Action
theory_units.summary: Execute a vertical pan to follow a subject's downward movement, beginning with an upward angle and tilting the camera down as the subject descends.
theory_units.applies_when: The director needs to show a subject moving downwards over a significant vertical distance, maintaining a continuous view.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys the smooth, uninterrupted motion of the subject and emphasizes the vertical scale of the environment.

theory_units.title: Shot Size Change: Dolly/Zoom vs. Cut
theory_units.summary: A change in shot size can be achieved either through continuous camera movement (dolly or zoom) or by transitioning abruptly to a new, differently framed shot (cut).
theory_units.applies_when: Deciding how to alter the proximity to a subject or detail within a sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dolly/zoom maintains continuity of space and emphasizes the *process* of getting closer/further, while a cut emphasizes the *result* and can imply a jump in time or a shift in focus.

theory_units.title: Continuous Crane Sequence Shot
theory_units.summary: A crane shot can be designed as a single, unbroken take that covers an entire sequence, replacing multiple cuts with continuous camera movement.
theory_units.applies_when: The director desires to emphasize continuous action, fluid transitions between different scales or perspectives, or create a sense of immersive, unbroken reality.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a powerful, immersive experience for the audience, enhances a sense of real-time progression, and can highlight complex choreography of action and camera.

theory_units.title: Simulating Motion with Camera Movement
theory_units.summary: Camera movement can be intentionally used to mimic or simulate the motion of the environment or subject (e.g., pitching deck of a ship, uneven ground), rather than just recording it.
theory_units.applies_when: The director wants to convey a character's physical experience, the instability of an environment, or create a specific sensory effect for the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a more visceral and subjective experience, making the audience feel as if they are experiencing the same motion as the character or scene. Enhances immersion and emotional connection.

theory_units.title: Shot Design for Emotional and Kinetic Quality
theory_units.summary: The specific design of a shot, including its size and composition, is crucial for conveying its emotional and kinetic qualities to the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning any shot where the emotional resonance or dynamic energy is a key objective, beyond mere logistical framing.
theory_units.expected_effect: A well-chosen shot size and composition will directly influence how the audience perceives the mood, intensity, and rhythm of a moment.
theory_units.caution: Relying solely on logistical schematics for planning may neglect critical qualitative aspects like emotional resonance and kinetic energy.

theory_units.title: Iterative Staging Refinement
theory_units.summary: Directors should iteratively refine the staging of characters and objects within a frame, often using visual aids like storyboards, until achieving desired compositional satisfaction.
theory_units.applies_when: During pre-production when planning the visual layout and blocking of a scene or shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Optimal visual balance, clarity, dramatic emphasis, or aesthetic satisfaction in the final composition.

theory_units.title: Visualizing for Dramatic Flow and Composition
theory_units.summary: Engaging in visual planning, such as storyboarding, helps directors understand the dramatic flow of a story, generate creative ideas, and effectively compose shots, offering insights not evident from the screenplay alone.
theory_units.applies_when: During early pre-production and script breakdown phases, as a director translates script into visual form.
theory_units.expected_effect: Improved narrative pacing, stronger shot compositions, discovery of new creative solutions, and a deeper conceptual grasp of the script's visual potential.
theory_units.caution: The quality of the drawing is less important than the thought process and engagement with visual composition it facilitates.

theory_units.title: Establishing Tone Through Mood and Composition
theory_units.summary: Directors can establish a film's tone by creating a specific mood, which can be achieved through techniques like ironic juxtaposition of setting or by using elegantly composed frames with simple shapes to evoke particular emotions or genre aesthetics.
theory_units.applies_when: Introducing a film or scene, especially when aiming to immediately convey its overarching emotional or stylistic identity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clear and effective communication of the film's tone, immediate emotional engagement from the audience, and genre resonance.

theory_units.title: Expressive Characters for Clear Intent
theory_units.summary: Employing highly expressive characters helps directors clearly convey the intended emotion, comedic timing, or dramatic purpose within each setup of a scene.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing actors, blocking character movements, or composing shots where a character's internal state or narrative role needs to be immediately understood.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhanced clarity of character intention, stronger emotional or comedic impact, and improved audience comprehension of character motivations and scene objectives.

theory_units.title: Motivated Angular Framing
theory_units.summary: Employ angular framing subtly and ensure it is fully motivated by the scene's staging to deepen audience relationship to characters, express a character's point of view, or establish mood.
theory_units.applies_when: When the goal is to create a nuanced subjective experience for the audience, enhance connection to characters' internal states (e.g., daydreaming), or contribute to the scene's specific tone.
theory_units.expected_effect: A subtle yet powerful communication of character subjectivity, emotional states, and audience relationship, without appearing artificial or unmotivated.
theory_units.caution: The angular framing must be subtle and directly motivated by the scene's staging to avoid distracting the audience or appearing unmotivated.

theory_units.title: Dramatic Backlighting and Shadow Effects
theory_units.summary: Utilize dramatic backlighting and evocative shadow effects to enhance the scene's mood, add visual drama, and reinforce character relationships or points of view.
theory_units.applies_when: When the narrative calls for heightened drama, a specific emotional tone, or when emphasizing a character's internal state or perspective (e.g., during daydreaming or intense moments).
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds visual depth and emotional resonance, contributing to the dramatic impact and helping to communicate subtle narrative elements like character relationships and subjective states.
theory_units.caution: Ensure lighting and shadow choices are in complete harmony with the subject and narrative intention, avoiding effects that feel gratuitous or unmotivated.

theory_units.title: Composition Serves Narrative Intention
theory_units.summary: All compositional choices, including the declaration of line and overall framing, must be in complete harmony with the subject and serve the narrative intention, never existing as an end in themselves.
theory_units.applies_when: Continuously, during all stages of visual design and direction; every compositional decision should be evaluated against its contribution to the story and subject.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures that the visual language of the film consistently supports and enhances the story, making the visual storytelling cohesive, impactful, and preventing superficiality.
theory_units.caution: Avoid making compositional choices solely for aesthetic appeal if they do not align with or actively detract from the narrative purpose.

theory_units.title: Shadow-Lead Character Reveal via Pan
theory_units.summary: Use a camera pan to follow a character's shadow, dynamically leading the audience's eye to the character's physical presence.
theory_units.applies_when: To introduce or bring attention to a character in a dynamic and visually engaging way, often utilizing a light source and the resulting shadow.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dynamically introduces or reveals a character, draws audience attention effectively, and can create a sense of mystery or intimacy.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful control of lighting and blocking to ensure the shadow is clear and leads effectively to the character.

theory_units.title: Visual Condensation of Story Elements
theory_units.summary: Combine multiple narrative or thematic elements into a single, potent visual image to convey information economically and evoke specific feelings.
theory_units.applies_when: When introducing key props, themes, or character traits that will become significant later in the narrative, and when aiming for concise and evocative exposition.
theory_units.expected_effect: Efficiently conveys complex information, enriches meaning, foreshadows future plot points, and evokes specific emotions (e.g., childhood innocence).
theory_units.caution: Ensure the combined image remains clear and decipherable to the audience; avoid over-complication that could lead to confusion.

theory_units.title: Streamlining by Omitting Transitional Shots
theory_units.summary: Enhance pacing and audience surprise by omitting redundant 'in-between' actions when the audience can infer the missing steps, especially if key props have already been introduced.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character performs an action (e.g., picking up a prop) that is easily inferable, and the prop's presence is already established; effective for quick reveals or surprises.
theory_units.expected_effect: Streamlines the scene, improves pacing, generates surprise without confusion, and focuses audience attention on essential moments.
theory_units.caution: The omitted action must be genuinely inferable to avoid confusing the audience or creating a sense of discontinuity.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Mirror Staging and Framing
theory_units.summary: Utilize reflections in multiple mirrors and dynamic set elements (e.g., swinging panels) to combine several perspectives, reveal actions, and frame character entrances within a single, continuous shot.
theory_units.applies_when: To visually integrate multiple actions or characters into one continuous shot, to create a sense of disorientation or dynamic tension, or to facilitate a surprising reveal of a character.
theory_units.expected_effect: Combines multiple 'shots' or perspectives into one, creates a unique visual dynamic, allows for complex character reveals (e.g., framing an entrance), and heightens the impact of an action. Can be executed so adroitly that the effect is seamless and 'all but invisible'.
theory_units.caution: Extremely complex to execute, requiring precise choreography of camera, actors, and set elements; can easily become confusing or overtly artificial if not handled subtly.

theory_units.title: Spielbergian Reflection Shot
theory_units.summary: Combine a character's face in semitransparent reflection with the external scene they are observing in a single shot, effectively merging a shot and reverse shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character is reacting to an external view through a window (e.g., car window) and the director wants to convey both the character's reaction and the object of their gaze simultaneously.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a visually complex and efficient shot that offers immediate insight into the character's perspective and reaction, potentially saving an edit and intensifying emotional connection.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the reflection and the external scene are both legible and contribute to the desired effect without becoming cluttered or confusing.

theory_units.title: Visual-First Script Development (Byrne Method)
theory_units.summary: Initiate script development by generating and arranging visual ideas (e.g., drawings on a wall) for scenes, and then layer dialogue, sound, and specific character details on top.
theory_units.applies_when: During the initial scriptwriting phase, particularly for director-writers, or when the goal is a highly visual narrative that prioritizes imagery alongside verbal content.
theory_units.expected_effect: Fosters a more cinematic script where visual and verbal elements are developed concurrently, potentially leading to more unconventional and visually driven narratives.
theory_units.caution: This method is personal and may not align with conventional script formats required by studios, which often prioritize a text-first approach.

theory_units.title: Visual Reference Scrapbook for Pre-production
theory_units.summary: Create and maintain a file or scrapbook of diverse images (e.g., photos, magazine clippings) for each scene or character during script composition and pre-production.
theory_units.applies_when: Throughout scriptwriting and early pre-production to reference specific locations, evoke memories and feelings, develop character backstories, and communicate the spirit and tone of scenes to the production designer and cinematographer.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enriches the dramatic content and texture of the story, aids in creating fully rounded characters, and provides concrete visual references that ensure consistent communication of the film's aesthetic to the crew.
theory_units.caution: The collected images serve as inspiration and mood setters; they do not necessarily have to represent actual planned shots for the film.

theory_units.title: Directing Actors via Analogy or Reference
theory_units.summary: Guide actor performances using broad, evocative analogies or real-life references (e.g., 'play it like Eleanor Roosevelt') instead of prescriptive line readings or specific gestures.
theory_units.applies_when: When an actor needs a deeper understanding of the character's essence or the scene's overall tone, or when direct, detailed instructions are proving less effective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Empowers the actor to internalize the role and discover their performance organically, leading to more nuanced, authentic, and less forced characterizations.
theory_units.caution: The chosen analogy must be well-understood by the actor and truly encapsulate the core intention of the character or scene; poorly chosen references can cause confusion.

theory_units.title: Music as a Visualization and Communication Tool
theory_units.summary: Utilize music during scriptwriting and pre-production to visualize a scene's mood and tempo, and to effectively communicate the desired rhythm and pace to department heads like production designers, cinematographers, and editors.
theory_units.applies_when: During script development, storyboarding, or collaborative meetings to establish the emotional atmosphere, temporal rhythm, and visual flow of a scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Instantly conveys complex emotional and temporal qualities, fostering a shared understanding among the crew and guiding the visual and aural execution of the scene.
theory_units.caution: The chosen music is for reference and communication; it doesn't have to be the final score, but it should accurately reflect the intended mood and rhythm to avoid misdirection.

theory_units.title: Practical Camera Skill Development
theory_units.summary: Regularly practice shooting with various cameras (Super 8, camcorders, still cameras) to hone visual skills, improve observational sensitivity, and understand how experience translates into images.
theory_units.applies_when: Continuously throughout a filmmaker's career, particularly during periods between major projects, to refine one's 'eye' and practical command of visual storytelling.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances the filmmaker's fundamental understanding of framing, composition, and visual language, making them a more intuitive and effective director of photography and storyteller.
theory_units.caution: The primary goal is skill development and observation, not necessarily to create polished final products; focus on the process of seeing and translating.

theory_units.title: Visual Testing During Location Scouting
theory_units.summary: Directors should actively test angles, compositions, and lenses during location scouts to bridge the gap between imagination and the final film's visual reality.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director is a 'visual stylist' and wants to proactively shape the visual look of the film, ensuring chosen locations work for specific shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Refines the visual plan, ensures chosen locations are suitable for specific shots, brings the director's visualization closer to the finished film's aesthetic.

theory_units.title: Illustrated Script for Visual Continuity
theory_units.summary: Create an 'illustrated script' by embedding photographs and/or concept sketches directly into the script to provide an overall visual overview for each scene.
theory_units.applies_when: During preproduction, especially after locations are secured, to maintain an overview of the film's pacing, mood, and visual arc, preventing a loss of perspective amidst production details.
theory_units.expected_effect: Helps the filmmaker gain a clear sense of the visual continuity for the entire film, ensuring pacing and mood are consistent across separately considered locations.

theory_units.title: Collaborative Visual Exploration (Overview Meetings)
theory_units.summary: Conduct overview meetings where the creative team collaboratively arranges and rearranges research material (photos, sketches, etc.) on a large surface to discover unexpected visual connections.
theory_units.applies_when: When the creative team needs to collectively explore visual ideas, find unexpected connections between disparate elements, and ensure visual choices directly impact the dramatic content.
theory_units.expected_effect: Encourages unexpected visual discoveries within the creative team, which directly impacts and enriches the dramatic content of the film.

theory_units.title: Relating Graphic Shot Qualities to Narrative Effects
theory_units.summary: A technique to heighten awareness of the relationship between visual and dramatic elements by rephrasing traditional graphic shot descriptions (position, size, angle, movement) into narrative questions.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning individual shots or scenes, to ensure that the photographic qualities chosen effectively serve and determine the desired narrative effect on the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Forces the director to see the material in new ways, ensuring that every visual decision has a clear narrative purpose and impact.

theory_units.title: Shot Size and Emotional Distance
theory_units.summary: The physical distance from a subject in a shot translates directly to emotional distance for the audience. Use greater distance to create emotional separation, emphasize inscrutability, or make the audience actively strain to perceive subtle character emotions.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming to depict emotional separation between characters and the audience, to maintain a character's inscrutability, or to invite audience engagement in discerning subtle emotions without explicit portrayal.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates emotional distance, makes a character appear inscrutable, forces the audience to actively seek and perceive subtle emotions on screen.
theory_units.caution: Using too much distance might make a character seem insignificant if not carefully balanced with narrative intent.

theory_units.title: Camera Angle for Communal Experience & Clear View
theory_units.summary: A medium high camera angle can effectively depict a group's shared, communal experience while simultaneously maintaining a clear view of a central figure or action, overcoming practical viewing obstructions.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting a shared experience of a group, focusing on a central figure within that group, and needing to overcome practical viewing obstacles (e.g., subjects blocking the camera's view from a lower angle).
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the shared group experience, provides a clear and encompassing view of the focal point, resolves practical blocking issues for the audience.
theory_units.caution: Too high an angle might diminish the emotional impact or relatability of the individual characters within the group.

theory_units.title: Sequence Shot for Slow, Solemn Development
theory_units.summary: Employing a continuous sequence shot, often with crane movement, is a deliberate choice to convey the slow, solemn development of an action and allow for a natural, shifting perspective without intrusive cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: When the scene's action should unfold slowly and deliberately, evoke a solemn or contemplative mood, and smoothly transition focus (e.g., from a group to an individual and back) while preserving continuity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of gravitas and unhurried pacing, provides an immersive and unbroken experience, allows for a smooth, natural shift in audience perspective.
theory_units.caution: Requires precise choreography of camera and subjects; if not well-executed, it can feel slow or draw attention to the camera rather than the action.

theory_units.title: Extreme Foreground Detail for Immersion/Context
theory_units.summary: Incorporating significant details or actions in the extreme foreground of a shot can ground the audience's perspective, add visual interest, and provide contextual character information.
theory_units.applies_when: When establishing a specific point of view (e.g., from one side of a conflict), to add visual texture, character context, or an immersive element that grounds the audience within the scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Grounds the audience's perspective within the scene, adds rich character detail and texture, enhances realism and visual interest.
theory_units.caution: Overly busy or distracting foreground elements can pull focus away from the main action or subject if not carefully composed.

theory_units.title: Low Angle for Establishing Importance/Arrival
theory_units.summary: Using a slightly low camera angle, particularly for an exterior long shot of an approaching character or group, can subtly emphasize their arrival, presence, or underlying importance.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character or group is making an entrance, to subtly convey their significance, gravitas, or the importance of the moment, even if their demeanor is unassuming or their actions mundane.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances the perceived presence, importance, or power of arriving characters, adding a subtle layer of narrative weight to their entrance.
theory_units.caution: Overuse can make characters seem overly dominant or artificial; should be used subtly if the intent is nuanced importance, not overt heroism.

theory_units.title: Camera Pull Back for Shifting Dynamics / Character Contrast
theory_units.summary: During or immediately following a significant character interaction, pulling the camera back can reveal broader spatial relationships, highlight shifting power dynamics, emphasize character contrasts (e.g., nervousness vs. composure), or introduce new elements into the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: During or after a crucial interaction (e.g., a handshake, a confrontation) to expand the scene's scope, show character reactions/dynamics, reveal subsequent actions, or contrast emotional states.
theory_units.expected_effect: Reveals broader scene dynamics and contextual information, highlights character contrasts, emphasizes subtle power shifts, and provides narrative context for unfolding events.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the pull-back serves a clear narrative or emotional purpose, rather than just being a decorative or gratuitous movement.

theory_units.title: Master Shot for Dialogue (Favoring Perspective)
theory_units.summary: Employ a wide, angular master shot that subtly favors one character during a dialogue scene to establish spatial relationships, capture the overall interaction, and influence audience perception by emphasizing that character's perspective or emotional state.
theory_units.applies_when: During a significant dialogue scene, especially when one character's presence, emotional state, or point of view should be subtly foregrounded while still showing the full interaction and scene geography.
theory_units.expected_effect: Establishes scene geography, provides a comprehensive view of the dialogue, and can subtly influence audience perception by favoring one character's importance or emotional impact without explicit close-ups.
theory_units.caution: Needs careful composition to ensure the 'favoring' feels natural and serves the narrative, rather than appearing as an arbitrary or distracting bias.

theory_units.title: Storyboard Text-Only Boxes for Sequence Thinking
theory_units.summary: Start storyboarding by writing out the shot plan in sequential boxes without drawings, which forces the director to focus on the cinematic flow and sequence of shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When translating a detailed shot plan into a storyboard, especially in the initial stages, to clarify the sequential order and pacing of shots before adding visual details.
theory_units.expected_effect: Improves cinematic thinking and understanding of shot order, making the shot list feel more like a screen sequence and identifying potential pacing issues.
theory_units.caution: This is an intermediate step; drawings or photos are still needed for full visualization and communication of specific compositions.

theory_units.title: Using Music/Rehearsal Dialogue for Storyboard Inspiration
theory_units.summary: Play music or recorded rehearsal dialogue while working on storyboards to stimulate imagination, suggest different ideas for pacing and mood, and deepen the emotional connection to the scene.
theory_units.applies_when: During storyboard creation or scene design, particularly for dramatic scenes, to generate fresh creative ideas and refine the emotional and rhythmic aspects of the scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Inspires new creative ideas, enhances understanding of pacing and mood, sharpens visualization skills, and improves the ability to judge what works for the scene's emotional impact.
theory_units.caution: Select music that aligns with the desired mood, or experiment with different tracks to explore a range of emotional possibilities; don't rely on music to fix fundamental scene issues.

theory_units.title: Using Models for Staging & Camera Planning
theory_units.summary: Employ models and miniature figures to plan complex scenes, test actor groupings, camera framing, and potential camera movements, including logistical elements behind the camera.
theory_units.applies_when: For complex scenes involving many extras, vehicles, or significant equipment (like cranes, dollies), or for detailed interior scenes, where logistical and staging challenges are high.
theory_units.expected_effect: Helps visualize logistics behind the camera, allows for perfection of staging, testing of specific shots and overviews, facilitates team communication, and provokes the filmmaker's imagination.
theory_units.caution: Models are most easily adapted to large complex scenes; the director should assess their appropriateness based on whether they effectively help perfect the scene without becoming overly time-consuming.

theory_units.title: Continuity of Shot Sizes
theory_units.summary: Long, medium, and close-up shots are treated as overlapping portions of a single space and are used together to create a consistent spatial/temporal order within a scene.
theory_units.applies_when: When sequencing different shot sizes (long, medium, close-up) within the continuity system.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience perceives a consistent and coherent spatial and temporal environment; shots make logical sense in relation to one another.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Visual Recognition Across Shot Sizes
theory_units.summary: When changing shot sizes, ensure that each subsequent shot is visually recognizable as an overlapping portion of the wider shot to avoid audience confusion.
theory_units.applies_when: When transitioning between shots of different scales.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience remains spatially oriented and does not get confused by changes in scale.
theory_units.caution: Historically, radical jumps (e.g., wide shot to close-up) without an intervening medium shot were considered too radical, but modern audiences are more accustomed to extreme changes in scale.

theory_units.title: Narrative Logic for Spatial Continuity
theory_units.summary: Narrative logic (cause and effect) and visual connection between shots cooperate to create a sense of continuous space, forming the organizational basis of the continuity style.
theory_units.applies_when: When constructing sequences where spatial continuity or cause-and-effect relationships need to be inferred or emphasized, especially if visual connection is not immediately obvious.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience perceives a continuous space and understands the narrative cause and effect, even if visual elements are not explicitly linked.

theory_units.title: Aesthetic Framing for Human Figures
theory_units.summary: Framing of human figures, particularly with long, medium, and close-up shots, is often guided by conventions of post-Renaissance art and principles of pleasing and balanced compositions.
theory_units.applies_when: Composing any shot featuring a human figure.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually balanced and aesthetically pleasing representation of the human form within the frame.

theory_units.title: Close-up for Intimacy and Action Emphasis
theory_units.summary: The close-up is used to bring the audience into closer contact with the action and subjects, often to compensate for smaller screen sizes and enhance intimacy.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring increased intimacy, emphasizing character emotion or action, or adapting for smaller screen formats (e.g., television).
theory_units.expected_effect: Greater audience intimacy with the subject and heightened focus on character or action.

theory_units.title: Predominant Dialogue Framing
theory_units.summary: The shoulder-and-head shot has become the predominant framing for dialogue sequences due to its balance of facial expression and efficiency.
theory_units.applies_when: Shooting dialogue scenes, particularly for ease of lighting and editing flexibility.
theory_units.expected_effect: Standard, recognizable framing that focuses on characters' faces and upper bodies during conversation, allowing for flexible editing.

theory_units.title: Eyes as a Spatial and Emotional Indicator
theory_units.summary: The eyes are the most expressive feature of the human face, communicating emotion and silently indicating interest in off-screen objects and their direction, thereby determining spatial relations.
theory_units.applies_when: Using a character's gaze to convey internal state (fear, interest) or to direct audience attention to off-screen elements and their location.
theory_units.expected_effect: Strong emotional communication, clear establishment of spatial relations, and effective guidance of audience gaze and anticipation.

theory_units.title: Importance of Accurate Eyeline Match
theory_units.summary: Viewers are highly sensitive to incongruities in sight lines between subjects looking at each other, easily detecting when an eye match is slightly off.
theory_units.applies_when: Shooting scenes where characters are looking at each other, especially during dialogue or direct interaction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Believable and natural interaction between characters, maintaining audience immersion.
theory_units.caution: Inaccurate eye matches are easily detected by the audience and can break their suspension of disbelief or create discomfort.

theory_units.title: Close-up as Intrusion or Shared Vulnerability
theory_units.summary: Close-ups manipulate social distance, capable of creating intense intimacy or making the audience feel as though they are intruding on privacy or sharing a moment of vulnerability.
theory_units.applies_when: Deliberately choosing the level of intimacy or discomfort the audience should feel towards a subject or situation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience feels an intimate connection, a sense of intrusion, discomfort, or shared vulnerability, fostering emotional involvement or detachment.
theory_units.caution: Overuse or inappropriate use can feel like a violation of privacy, forcing intimacy without consent, potentially making viewers uncomfortable.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Off-Center Sequencing
theory_units.summary: Using off-center compositions in alternating close-ups creates a dynamic left/right eye motion for the audience, an effect that becomes more pronounced with wider screen aspect ratios.
theory_units.applies_when: Sequencing multiple close-up shots, particularly in wider aspect ratios, to create visual dynamism and rhythm.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dynamic visual rhythm, encouraging audience's eyes to move across the screen, leading to increased engagement.
theory_units.caution: Dead-center compositions in sequence can result in a lack of visual rhythm, causing the eyes to remain focused on the screen's center.

theory_units.title: Off-Center Portrait Framing (Western Art)
theory_units.summary: Western art conventions for portraits favor positioning the human face slightly off-center, typically leaving more space in the direction of the subject's gaze ('look room') and more space at the bottom of the frame than at the top.
theory_units.applies_when: Composing portraits of human faces, especially when aiming for conventionally pleasing or balanced aesthetics influenced by Western art traditions.
theory_units.expected_effect: An aesthetically pleasing, balanced, and non-symmetrical composition that guides the viewer's eye.
theory_units.caution: These are conventions and should not limit artistic experimentation if they do not suit the filmmaker's specific design or style.

theory_units.title: Sharply Off-Center Framing for Modern Aesthetics
theory_units.summary: Sharply off-center framing is a viable compositional choice, with its effect becoming more pronounced in wider screens, influenced by contemporary print advertising and modern graphics.
theory_units.applies_when: Desiring a contemporary, dynamic, or unconventional portrait composition, especially in wide aspect ratios, or to evoke a commercial/graphic sensibility.
theory_units.expected_effect: A pronounced, modern visual effect that can feel fresh and dynamic, drawing on current advertising aesthetics.
theory_units.caution: While common, this style should be employed intentionally to serve the film's specific design and desired visual impact.

theory_units.title: Macro Close-ups for Narrative and Sensory Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Extreme or macro close-ups of specific facial features (eyes, mouth, ears) are frequently used to advance the narrative, highlight sensory information, or emphasize specific emotions.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to draw the audience's attention to a critical narrative detail, a specific sensory experience (e.g., faint sound), or an intense emotion tied to a particular feature.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightened focus on a specific narrative element or sensory input, amplification of emotion, and increased suspense or intimacy.
theory_units.caution: Traditional viewpoints (front or side) are common, but experimentation with unconventional viewpoints, framing, and shot size is encouraged to explore texture, light, and form.

theory_units.title: Medium Shot for Comprehensive Performance Capture
theory_units.summary: The medium shot combines qualities of the full shot and close-up, effectively capturing an actor's gestures and body language while remaining tight enough to include subtle facial expressions.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to show a broader scope of character performance (e.g., gestures, posture) alongside facial reactions and emotional nuance.
theory_units.expected_effect: A comprehensive view of character performance, balancing physical action with emotional depth.
theory_units.caution: Currently shares popularity with close-ups and is not typically used as the sole or primary setup for an entire scene alone.

theory_units.title: Medium Shot for Group Dialogue Composition
theory_units.summary: The medium shot serves as the general range for composing group dialogue scenes, typically accommodating two to five players.
theory_units.applies_when: Composing scenes involving dialogue between multiple characters (typically 2-5).
theory_units.expected_effect: A clear presentation of multiple characters in conversation, maintaining a suitable distance for interaction while allowing for some individual expression.
theory_units.caution: For scenes with more than five players, the camera often needs to pull back to a full-shot range to include everyone, unless the figures are significantly overlapped.

theory_units.title: Full Shot for Establishing Location and Character
theory_units.summary: The full shot serves as an establishing shot to connect a character with their location in a single frame, especially when tighter shots are considered but broader context is needed.
theory_units.applies_when: When it is necessary to clearly establish or connect a character and their surrounding location within one shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides immediate spatial context, grounding the character within their environment and setting the scene.
theory_units.caution: This use of the full shot has fallen into disuse for primary dialogue scenes, often being relegated to initial scene setup.

theory_units.title: Full Shot for Actor Body Language
theory_units.summary: A full shot allows actors to utilize their entire body for expression, enabling the communication of subtle non-verbal cues and physical performance.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director wants to emphasize or allow an actor's full range of physical expression and body language to convey meaning, rather than solely relying on facial expressions or dialogue.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enriches character performance by adding nuance through physical presence, providing the audience with a broader understanding of emotions and intentions.
theory_units.caution: Requires dialogue scenes to be played in long takes to maximize the effect, which can be less common in modern filmmaking due to production preferences and cost.

theory_units.title: Asymmetrical Framing in Full Shots of Single Figures
theory_units.summary: Full shots of a single figure offer opportunities for asymmetrical framing, particularly in wider formats, allowing for dynamic graphic patterns within the composition.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing a full shot of a single standing figure, especially in wider aspect ratios, and seeking to create a visually dynamic or graphically strong composition.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a more dynamic, visually interesting composition by emphasizing graphic lines and potentially generating visual tension or balance through off-center placement.
theory_units.caution: While asymmetrical framing can be powerful, a centered subject can also be effective; the choice should be intentional based on desired impact.

theory_units.title: The Line of Action (180-Degree Rule)
theory_units.summary: The 180-degree rule dictates that an imaginary 'line of action' is drawn between subjects, and all camera positions must remain within a 180-degree semicircle on one side of this line to preserve consistent screen direction and space.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming any scene (especially dialogue) that requires multiple camera angles to be cut together, where maintaining clear and consistent screen direction and spatial relationships for the audience is crucial.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents audience disorientation by ensuring consistent screen direction (e.g., characters always looking at each other from the same side of the screen) and clear spatial understanding of character positions.
theory_units.caution: Crossing the line (placing cameras outside the 180-degree semicircle) will result in a confusing reversal of left and right screen space, disorienting the viewer.

theory_units.title: Triangle System for Basic Camera Coverage
theory_units.summary: The Triangle System is a shorthand method for camera placement within the 180-degree rule, proposing that all basic shots for a subject can be obtained from three strategic points within the 180-degree working space.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning camera setups for dialogue scenes or action sequences in the continuity style, aiming for comprehensive basic shot coverage while adhering to the 180-degree rule.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a systematic, efficient, and versatile way to obtain a full range of basic shots (singles, two-shots, over-the-shoulder, POV, profiles) while ensuring consistent screen direction and spatial relationships.
theory_units.caution: While adaptable for single or multiple cameras, extensive staging or camera movement might be restricted in a multi-camera setup to avoid cameras moving in front of each other.

theory_units.title: Establishing a New Line of Action via Pivot Shot
theory_units.summary: A new line of action, allowing cameras to cross the original line, can be established by a 'pivot shot' where a character turns their attention to a new person or area within the frame, creating a new line of sight.
theory_units.applies_when: When the narrative requires a shift in focus or spatial orientation, and the director needs to move camera positions across the original line of action without disorienting cuts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Facilitates a smooth and logical transition across the original line of action, clearly signaling to the audience the shift in spatial relationships and opening up a new 180-degree working space for the camera.
theory_units.caution: While a return to an old line of action might not always require a new pivot shot if spatial geography is clear, conventional wisdom advocates reusing lines for consistent space.

theory_units.title: Establishing a New Line of Action via Player Movement
theory_units.summary: A new line of action can be established by having a character physically cross their own line of action in a clearly depicted shot, which effectively reorients the viewer to a new 180-degree working space.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character's physical movement in a scene naturally leads to a shift in spatial dynamics, requiring a new line of action to be established.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for dynamic character movement and corresponding camera reorientation while maintaining spatial clarity for the audience, by showing the continuous action of the character changing position.
theory_units.caution: The actor's relocation must be clearly seen in a shot that allows the viewer to easily reorient themselves to the new spatial arrangement.

theory_units.title: Centering Camera for Dialogue in Confined Spaces
theory_units.summary: When choosing the 180-degree working area for a new line of action, particularly in dialogue situations at a table or within a confined space, the camera should generally be kept in the center of the group.
theory_units.applies_when: Establishing or choosing the camera's 180-degree working space in dialogue situations occurring at a table or within any other confined setting.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains clear spatial relationships between characters and provides natural, inclusive framing for group interactions, enhancing audience understanding of who is speaking to whom.
theory_units.caution: The specific angle and shot size can vary, but the general working area choice supports group dialogue clarity.

theory_units.title: Crossing the Line via Uninterrupted Camera Movement
theory_units.summary: The camera can cross the line of action via an uninterrupted pan, dolly, or crane move, establishing a new line of action without disorienting the viewer because the continuous movement visually reorients them.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director desires a fluid, continuous shift in perspective that crosses the line of action without a cut, allowing for a dynamic spatial reorientation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a smooth, dynamic transition to a new spatial arrangement; the continuous camera movement inherently prevents audience disorientation that would occur with a direct cut across the line.
theory_units.caution: The camera movement must remain uninterrupted throughout the line-crossing for the effect to be successful and clear.

theory_units.title: Crossing the Line via Cutaway or Bridge Shot
theory_units.summary: A cutaway shot, which is related to the action but not specifically tied to the scene's immediate geography, can be used to 'bridge' a cut across the line of action without disorienting the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: When other methods of crossing the line (pivot shot, character movement, camera movement) are not feasible or appropriate within the scene's action, or as a 'quick fix' in editing when continuity problems arise.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for a discreet and non-disorienting jump across the line of action by momentarily diverting the viewer's attention from the main scene geography before returning to a new camera position.
theory_units.caution: The cutaway shot must be 'clearly related to the action' to avoid feeling arbitrary or confusing to the viewer.

theory_units.title: Deliberate Line Crossing for Dynamic Action Sequences
theory_units.summary: For fast-moving subjects or action sequences, intentionally crossing the line of action and reversing screen direction can sometimes yield more dynamic and interesting results, as modern viewers are often visually sophisticated enough to interpret it.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming fast-moving subjects or intense action sequences where strict adherence to the 180-degree rule might limit creative options or hinder the desired dynamic impact of the sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a more energetic, exciting, or visually engaging sequence, prioritizing kinetic impact or artistic expression over strict screen direction continuity.
theory_units.caution: May result in a reversal of screen direction, which could potentially confuse some viewers or detract from spatial clarity if not executed thoughtfully or if the audience is not highly visually literate.

theory_units.title: Line of Action for Moving Subjects (Motion-Based)
theory_units.summary: In action sequences where a clear line of sight between characters is absent or irrelevant, the line of action is established by following the dominant path of motion of the subject.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming action sequences involving significant movement, particularly when there is no clear interaction or 'line of sight' between characters to establish the line of action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains consistent screen direction for moving subjects (e.g., a car chase), aiding viewer comprehension of their trajectory and interactions within the space, even without dialogue.
theory_units.caution: This rule should be applied carefully; for complex scenarios, 'implied sight lines' or deliberate crossing may be considered.

theory_units.title: Implied Sight Line for Vehicles Moving Alongside
theory_units.summary: When two vehicles or conveyances with drivers are moving alongside each other, an 'implied sight line' can be established between them as an additional line of action, temporarily overriding the line of motion.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming two vehicles (or other conveyances with drivers) moving side-by-side, especially during dialogue or interaction between the occupants, even if the drivers are not prominent.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for dynamic cutting between the vehicles while maintaining a sense of eye-line continuity, treating the vehicles as symbols of the drivers and their spatial relationship, despite movement.
theory_units.caution: Shots photographed from both sides of the *line of motion* will still result in a reversal of screen direction when cut together, but the implied sight line offers latitude for dialogue within this.

theory_units.title: Establishing New Line in Action: Subject Crosses Line
theory_units.summary: In action sequences, a subject physically crossing the established line of motion (e.g., a car changing lanes) establishes a new line of action based on its subsequent direction of movement.
theory_units.applies_when: An action sequence where a moving subject's change of trajectory or position dynamically redefines the spatial orientation, allowing for new camera setups across the old line of action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dynamically redefines screen space and direction by visually demonstrating the continuous action of the subject moving across the line, guiding the audience's spatial understanding.
theory_units.caution: The subject's movement across the line must be clearly depicted to enable the viewer to reorient themselves to the new line of action.

theory_units.title: Establishing New Line in Action: Camera Crosses Line
theory_units.summary: In action sequences, the camera can cross the line of motion through an uninterrupted pan, dolly, or crane move to a new space, thereby establishing a new line of action without disorienting cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: An action sequence where a fluid, continuous camera movement is desired to change perspective, cover new scene space, and redefine the line of action without cutting.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic shift in viewpoint and reorients the audience smoothly by showing the camera's continuous journey across the line of action, enhancing the sense of movement and immersion.
theory_units.caution: The camera movement must be uninterrupted for the effect to work; sudden cuts across the line are not permissible with this strategy.

theory_units.title: Establishing New Line in Action: New Subject Enters
theory_units.summary: In action sequences, the entry of a new subject into the frame that becomes the dominant line of motion can establish a new line of action for the scene.
theory_units.applies_when: An action sequence where a new participant or element (e.g., another car in a chase) shifts the focus and spatial dynamics, necessitating a new line of action for subsequent camera placements.
theory_units.expected_effect: Redefines the spatial relationships and screen direction based on the new dominant motion, integrating the new subject seamlessly into the scene's geography and allowing for continued coherent coverage.
theory_units.caution: The new subject's entry and its establishment as the dominant line of motion should be clearly communicated visually.

theory_units.title: Screen Direction Reversal with Profile Shots
theory_units.summary: When the camera crosses the line of action and the subject is shown in profile, the resulting reversal of screen direction can be more startling and disorienting.
theory_units.applies_when: When editing shots where the camera has crossed the line of action and the subject is in profile.
theory_units.expected_effect: An increased sense of disorientation or a 'startling' visual effect on the audience compared to front/back views.
theory_units.caution: This effect is more pronounced and potentially jarring, which may not always be desired.

theory_units.title: Differentiating Shots with Front and Back Views
theory_units.summary: If the subject's sight line is aligned with the line of action, using front and back views helps the viewer differentiate shots even when the line of action is crossed.
theory_units.applies_when: When shooting on the line of action where screen direction reversal might occur, and clarity of spatial relationship is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Helps viewers maintain geographical understanding and differentiate between shots, reducing potential confusion.

theory_units.title: Establishing Causal Connections in Plot
theory_units.summary: Editing can establish a causal connection between events, transforming a mere series of actions into a coherent plot by prompting the audience to make logical connections.
theory_units.applies_when: When structuring a narrative to create a plot rather than just a sequence of disparate events.
theory_units.expected_effect: Involves the audience in making logical connections, provokes speculation, and deepens engagement with the story.

theory_units.title: Temporal Continuity Connection
theory_units.summary: Connects two shots by showing an action in the first shot immediately followed by its temporal consequence in the second shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting an action and its immediate temporal result across a cut to maintain narrative flow.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates the illusion of a real, physical world and establishes clear temporal continuity.

theory_units.title: Spatial Continuity Connection
theory_units.summary: Connects two shots by cutting from a wider view of a location to a recognizable detail within that same location.
theory_units.applies_when: When establishing or reinforcing the spatial environment of a scene, or guiding viewer attention within a space.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates the illusion of a real, physical world, establishes clear spatial continuity, and helps viewers orient themselves within the scene.

theory_units.title: Logical Implied Connection
theory_units.summary: Connects two shots by relying on the audience's recognition and inference to bridge a logical gap, without requiring direct temporal or spatial overlap.
theory_units.applies_when: When implying a relationship between subjects, locations, or concepts where direct temporal or spatial connections are not necessary or desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows the audience to make inferences, creates a coherent world without explicit exposition, and can be more efficient in storytelling.
theory_units.caution: Relies on clear recognition and inference; if elements are not sufficiently clear, it could confuse the audience.

theory_units.title: Driving Narrative with Expectations (Narrative Motion)
theory_units.summary: Devising editing strategies that set up a framework of expectations in a series of shots, by asking questions and setting up anticipated answers, to propel the story forward.
theory_units.applies_when: Throughout narrative film to keep the audience actively engaged and to advance the plot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Engages the audience by encouraging speculation and anticipation, creating a sense of 'narrative motion' and forward momentum.

theory_units.title: Simplest Observer-Object Q&A Pattern
theory_units.summary: A basic two-shot editing pattern where a shot of a person looking offscreen is followed by a shot of the object they are observing.
theory_units.applies_when: To establish what a character is looking at, to direct audience attention, or to initiate a simple question-and-answer sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clarifies the character's focus, builds a simple question ('What are they looking at?') and provides an immediate answer.

theory_units.title: Suspenseful Q&A Reversal (Audience Privilege)
theory_units.summary: Creating suspense by placing an answer (revealing information) before the question (a character's discovery or search for that information), thus placing the audience in a privileged position.
theory_units.applies_when: When the filmmaker wants the audience to share a 'secret' or be in a privileged, often uncomfortable, position regarding a character's impending discovery.
theory_units.expected_effect: Builds suspense as the audience knows what will happen before the character, creating anticipation and tension, and implicating the viewer.

theory_units.title: Postponing Answers for Tension
theory_units.summary: A question raised in one shot is not immediately answered in the subsequent shot, but several shots later, building tension or suspense.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director wants to prolong suspense, divert attention, or emphasize intervening actions before revealing the answer to a posed question.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increases viewer engagement and anticipation by delaying gratification, creates a sense of prolonged tension.
theory_units.caution: Overuse or excessively long delays might frustrate or confuse the audience if the question is lost or its urgency diminishes.

theory_units.title: Presenting Answer Before Question
theory_units.summary: The object of attention or the answer to a future question is shown before the character explicitly poses the question or shows interest.
theory_units.applies_when: To create specific dramatic or comedic effects by revealing information before a character's reaction or search, setting up an ironic distance or anticipation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Can create dramatic irony, immediate intrigue, or a specific kind of suspense (where the audience knows more than the character).
theory_units.caution: May reduce immediate mystery surrounding the object if not used carefully, as the answer is given preemptively.

theory_units.title: Elaborating Questions for Incremental Reveal
theory_units.summary: A question is raised and then elaborated upon through a series of partial answers or details across multiple shots before a complete answer is provided.
theory_units.applies_when: When building a mystery, gradually revealing character or plot details, or involving the viewer in a deductive process.
theory_units.expected_effect: Engages the viewer in solving the 'mystery' alongside the narrative, builds intrigue and anticipation through a slow drip of information.
theory_units.caution: Too many partial answers or an excessively long elaboration might diffuse the question's urgency or overwhelm the viewer.

theory_units.title: Dense Multiple Q&A Patterns
theory_units.summary: Raising and answering multiple questions simultaneously or in quick succession within the same shot or series of shots, creating a complex and layered narrative.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming to create rich, complex psychological fiction, to implicate the viewer in moral dilemmas, or to maximize information density within a sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a highly engaging and challenging viewing experience, encourages active viewer interpretation, and deepens narrative complexity.
theory_units.caution: Can be confusing if not executed with extreme clarity and careful planning; carries the risk of overwhelming the audience.

theory_units.title: Question-Raising Scene Introductions
theory_units.summary: Introducing a scene or location not with a predictable establishing shot, but with a sequence of fragmented shots that raise questions, actively engaging the viewer.
theory_units.applies_when: When the goal is to engage the viewer immediately and contribute to narrative motion, rather than merely provide spatial orientation passively.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightens viewer engagement by making them actively connect pieces of information, creates intrigue, and avoids passive viewing often associated with conventional establishing shots.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful planning to ensure the fragmented shots eventually cohere into a meaningful understanding of the location without causing confusion.

theory_units.title: Manipulating Audience Assumptions
theory_units.summary: Filmmakers can strategically support or subvert audience assumptions (e.g., about morality, character roles, or storytelling conventions) to achieve profound dramatic or psychological effects.
theory_units.applies_when: When seeking to shock, surprise, unsettle, or deeply engage the audience by playing against established narrative norms or moral expectations (e.g., killing the perceived protagonist).
theory_units.expected_effect: Shocks and disorients the audience, making them question the fictional world's rules and their own assumptions, leading to deeper emotional impact or engagement.
theory_units.caution: Risks alienating the audience if subversion feels gratuitous or unjustified, potentially breaking their trust in the narrative.

theory_units.title: Basic Coverage System
theory_units.summary: A system of shooting multiple camera setups (wide, medium, close-up) for every action to ensure that a logical sequence can be cut together in editing.
theory_units.applies_when: When prioritizing a safe shoot, ensuring continuity, or needing maximum flexibility in the editing room. Often used when the director has gambled on an unusual approach.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures a logical sequence can be cut together, provides backup shots, covers potential issues with more ambitious single shots.
theory_units.caution: Can lead to uninspired visuals if specific visual strategies are discouraged in favor of generic coverage; time constraints may prevent more ambitious visual approaches.

theory_units.title: Shooting Backup Shots
theory_units.summary: After essential shots are filmed and the set is lit and blocked, additional angles are captured rapidly to provide extra safety and flexibility.
theory_units.applies_when: When a set is already lit and blocked, essential shots are complete, and time permits, or when a director wants to hedge against risks of an unusual approach.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides practical insurance against errors or unforeseen editing needs, gives more options for the editor.
theory_units.caution: Can potentially lead to excess footage if not managed by an experienced director.

theory_units.title: Hiding Cuts on Action
theory_units.summary: To preserve continuity and hide the edit, cuts between different views of a subject are made somewhere *into* the action rather than before or after it completes.
theory_units.applies_when: When combining two or more camera angles of a subject performing an action (e.g., lifting a drink, turning head, jumping).
theory_units.expected_effect: Hides the cut, makes the transition to a new shot invisible, maintains a smooth flow of action.
theory_units.caution: The exact point depends on the subject and editor's sense of movement; cutting too early or late can make the cut noticeable.

theory_units.title: Staging for Action Cuts
theory_units.summary: Filmmakers should stage action so it overlaps an anticipated edit point between camera angles, allowing for smooth cuts on movement.
theory_units.applies_when: During the staging and blocking phase, when planning for sequences that will utilize cutting on movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates clear opportunities for editors to make invisible cuts, ensuring visual motivation for edits.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful pre-visualization and coordination between director and editor's perspective.

theory_units.title: Cutting on Partial Exits/Entrances
theory_units.summary: When a subject moves into or out of a frame, the cut is made while the subject is still partially within the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: A subject is entering or exiting the frame in a sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Makes the cut smoother, speeds up the flow of action onscreen.

theory_units.title: Clearing the Frame (Full Exit)
theory_units.summary: A subject is allowed to completely exit the frame before a cut is made to a new shot. It is customary to hold on the empty frame of the outgoing shot for a moment (minimum 1-2 seconds).
theory_units.applies_when: As an alternative to cutting on movement, especially when joining different angles of the same subject, or when indicating a passage of time or change in background.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a flexible cut that is almost impossible to make a continuity mistake with, can join shots on opposite sides of the line of action, can indicate passage of time, or allow an empty frame to serve as an establishing shot.
theory_units.caution: Opening the incoming shot with the subject already in frame is less common in continuity style and can feel abrupt.

theory_units.title: Clearing the Frame (Delayed Entry)
theory_units.summary: The outgoing shot ends with the subject clearly within the frame. The incoming shot begins with an empty frame and holds for at least a second before the subject enters.
theory_units.applies_when: When transitioning between shots where a slight pause or anticipation before the subject's re-entry is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Can create anticipation, potentially smooths the transition by creating a brief visual 'rest' or reset.

theory_units.title: Establishing Location (Wide to Close)
theory_units.summary: Establish a location by starting with a wide shot and progressively moving closer to the subject or key detail through a sequence of varying shot sizes.
theory_units.applies_when: When introducing a new location or moving from a general overview to a specific point of interest, guiding the viewer's attention.
theory_units.expected_effect: Guides the viewer's eye, clarifies spatial relationships, creates a sense of moving into the scene, can vary velocity and acceleration depending on shot size jumps.
theory_units.caution: Limited change between frames in initial shots can create less dynamism if shots are too similar in scale.

theory_units.title: Establishing Location (Close to Wide - Pullback)
theory_units.summary: Establish a location by starting with a close-up of a detail and gradually pulling back (or cutting to wider shots) to reveal the full location.
theory_units.applies_when: When starting with an intriguing detail and then revealing its broader context within a location, or to create a sense of 'pulling back' from a subject.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of discovery, reveals the environment around a detail, provides context, can make a wide jump through space while retaining spatial unity.

theory_units.title: Establishing Location (Details to Whole)
theory_units.summary: Establish a location by presenting a series of close-ups or details from which the viewer constructs an understanding of the whole place, relying on iconographic images.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming for a more iconographic, abstract representation of a location, or to convey mood and atmosphere through specific elements rather than a direct overview.
theory_units.expected_effect: Engages the viewer to piece together the environment, conveys mood and story through selected details, can be very evocative.
theory_units.caution: Relies heavily on the viewer's interpretation; may not immediately provide clear spatial orientation unless details are carefully chosen.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Pullback with Angle Change
theory_units.summary: Combine a pullback sequence (from CU to wide) with a significant and often unexpected jump in camera angle, frequently ending with an angular aerial shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When performing a pullback sequence and desiring a strong visual contrast and more dynamic effect, especially when breaking an expected straight line of motion.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic editing pattern, adds visual energy, breaks visual expectation, provides a powerful graphic effect.

theory_units.title: Establishing Wider Context
