theory_units.summary: To effectively introduce the period, characters, and mood of a scene, the initial shot should provide a wider context beyond the immediate subject.
theory_units.applies_when: When opening a scene or sequence that needs to establish setting, time, and atmosphere.
theory_units.expected_effect: Helps the audience immediately grasp the broader environment, period, and emotional tone of the story.

theory_units.title: High-Angle for Emotional Distance
theory_units.summary: Using a high-angle shot can create a slight sense of removal or distance between the audience and the action.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to slightly detach the viewer from the immediate emotional intensity or action.
theory_units.expected_effect: A more objective or observational perspective for the audience, providing 'breathing room'.
theory_units.caution: Can be perceived as less immediate or less engaging if not used intentionally.

theory_units.title: Surrounding Space for Breathing Room
theory_units.summary: Including more surrounding space in a shot can give the audience a feeling of 'breathing room'.
theory_units.applies_when: When a scene feels too cramped or visually intense, or when aiming for a more relaxed or open mood.
theory_units.expected_effect: A sense of openness, relaxation, or less confinement for the viewer.

theory_units.title: Tighter Framing for Improvement
theory_units.summary: Adjusting framing to be tighter can often improve a shot's focus and impact.
theory_units.applies_when: When a shot feels too loose, contains distracting elements, or needs to emphasize a particular detail or subject more strongly.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased visual clarity, emphasis on the subject, and potentially greater impact.
theory_units.caution: Overly tight framing can feel claustrophobic or omit important contextual information.

theory_units.title: Low-Angle for Specific Subjects
theory_units.summary: Employing a low-angle shot for particular subjects can create a specific visual or emotional effect.
theory_units.applies_when: When highlighting an object or person, often to give it significance, power, or a unique visual perspective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Can make the subject appear larger, more imposing, or draw specific attention to it.

theory_units.title: Establishing Area with Lower Viewpoint and Pan
theory_units.summary: Begin with a lower viewpoint to capture a broader area like a neighborhood, then pan down to reveal a specific location, such as a house.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to first establish a general environment or context before narrowing the focus to a specific element within it.
theory_units.expected_effect: Gradually introduces the setting, building a sense of place from broad to specific.

theory_units.title: Intercutting to Broaden Focus
theory_units.summary: Intercutting new characters into a sequence can broaden the narrative scope and break focus from a singular action or set of characters.
theory_units.applies_when: When the narrative is too narrowly focused or needs to introduce other family members or elements into a busy scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Diversifies the audience's attention, introduces more characters, and can make a scene feel more dynamic or 'hectic'.
theory_units.caution: Could potentially distract from a primary storyline if not handled carefully.

theory_units.title: Maintain Character Point of View
theory_units.summary: After an initial establishing shot, the point of view of a scene should consistently move to and remain with a specific character to engage the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: Once the initial context is established, to deepen the audience's connection with a character and experience the scene through their eyes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Strengthens audience empathy and understanding of the character's perspective within the scene.
theory_units.caution: Losing consistent POV can disconnect the audience from the character's experience.

theory_units.title: Frontal Staging for Single Master
theory_units.summary: Staging actors in a frontal position (facing the camera) allows for a scene to be covered effectively with a single master shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When shooting a dialogue scene and desiring to capture all actors within one continuous shot, or to minimize camera setups.
theory_units.expected_effect: Simplifies coverage and maintains a continuous, unbroken spatial relationship for the audience.
theory_units.caution: Can appear less naturalistic as actors face the camera more than each other; may limit close-up opportunities.

theory_units.title: Multiple Angles for Non-Frontal Staging
theory_units.summary: If actors are turned away from the camera (partially or completely), multiple camera angles are necessary to capture both actors' faces in dialogue.
theory_units.applies_when: When actors are positioned more naturally facing each other, rather than the camera, during a dialogue scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the audience can see the reactions and expressions of all speaking characters, often leading to a more naturalistic feel.
theory_units.caution: Requires more camera setups and relies on editing to convey the full scene.

theory_units.title: Static Master for Planned Coverage
theory_units.summary: A master shot should typically remain motionless if the director intends to cut to other camera angles later for coverage.
theory_units.applies_when: When a master shot is used as part of a broader coverage plan for a scene, to provide a stable foundation for later cuts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a consistent spatial reference point for editing, making cuts to other angles smoother and less disorienting.
theory_units.caution: A moving master shot can complicate editing with other angles if not meticulously planned.

theory_units.title: Sequence Shot (Moving Master)
theory_units.summary: A 'sequence shot' is a moving master shot where the camera fluidly repositions, often with a dolly and actor movement, to combine multiple angles without cutting.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director wants to maintain a continuous, unbroken shot through a scene, fluidly guiding the audience's attention and spatial understanding.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic, immersive experience, combining the information of several shots into one continuous flow.
theory_units.caution: Difficult to execute effectively; tends to maintain a general viewing direction and avoids quick 180-degree changes due to spatial continuity challenges.

theory_units.title: Medium Two-Shot for Relaxed Framing
theory_units.summary: The medium two-shot is a 'relaxed framing device' that can effectively cover entire dialogue sequences.
theory_units.applies_when: Particularly effective for comedies and musicals, or any scene where a relaxed, observational tone is desired without needing extreme close-ups.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a comfortable, easy-to-watch framing that allows interaction between characters to unfold naturally.
theory_units.caution: May not provide the intimacy or specific emotional emphasis of a close-up.

theory_units.title: Full/Medium Shots for Body Language
theory_units.summary: Full and medium shots are excellent for capturing expressive body movement and how characters relate to each other through their physical presence.
theory_units.applies_when: When body language, posture, movement, and spatial relationships between characters are key to conveying emotion or narrative information.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows the audience to perceive nuanced character relationships and expressions through physical cues, offering objectivity and detail.
theory_units.caution: May not convey individual character's internal thoughts or isolated emotional reactions as effectively as a close-up.

theory_units.title: Shot, Reverse Shot Pattern
theory_units.summary: The shot, reverse shot pattern is a highly useful solution for portraying alternating close-ups in dialogue scenes.
theory_units.applies_when: When two or more characters are engaging in dialogue and the director wants to emphasize individual reactions and shift point of view.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows the audience to see isolated reactions, changes the point of view within the scene, and uses eye-line matches to maintain spatial unity.
theory_units.caution: Overuse can become predictable; requires careful management of the 180-degree rule.

theory_units.title: Sight Line Proximity and Audience Intimacy
theory_units.summary: The closer an actor's sight line is to the camera, the more intimate the audience's connection will be with that actor.
theory_units.applies_when: When directing an actor's gaze in a shot to control the level of intimacy or connection the audience feels with them.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directly influences the audience's perceived closeness or psychological involvement with the character.
theory_units.caution: Too close (direct eye contact) can be startling or break immersion if not intended.

theory_units.title: Direct Eye Contact for Confrontation
theory_units.summary: An actor looking directly into the camera lens (direct eye contact) creates a confrontational and startling relationship with the viewer.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director specifically wants to directly engage, confront, or startle the audience, breaking the illusion of the film world.
theory_units.expected_effect: A powerful, often shocking or intrusive, effect that forces the audience to acknowledge their role as viewers.
theory_units.caution: Should be used sparingly and intentionally, as it can break immersion and disrupt narrative flow if not carefully justified.

theory_units.title: Direct Eye Contact for Subjective Camera
theory_units.summary: Direct eye contact is frequently used in subjective camera sequences to make the audience see things through the eyes of a character.
theory_units.applies_when: When creating a first-person perspective, where the audience is meant to embody a character's gaze and experience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Deepens immersion and empathy by literally putting the audience in the character's shoes, often used to convey psychological states.
theory_units.caution: Relatively infrequent in narrative film; requires careful handling to avoid confusion about whose POV is being shown.

theory_units.title: Standard Dialogue Sight Lines
theory_units.summary: In most dialogue scenes, actors' sight lines are directed slightly to the left or right of the camera, rather than directly into it.
theory_units.applies_when: During standard dialogue scenes to maintain the illusion of characters interacting with each other, not the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a naturalistic and immersive viewing experience where the audience feels like an observer, not a participant in the conversation.
theory_units.caution: Deviating significantly can lead to an unnatural or disconnected feeling for the audience.

theory_units.title: Consistent Sight Line Distance in Alternating Close-ups
theory_units.summary: In alternating close-ups of two or more actors, it is common practice to maintain the same distance from the camera for their respective sight lines.
theory_units.applies_when: When cutting between individual close-ups of characters in a dialogue scene to preserve spatial continuity and visual balance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures a smooth, spatially coherent editing rhythm, preventing visual jarring or a sense of mismatched perspectives between shots.
theory_units.caution: Inconsistent sight line distances can disorient the audience or make the cuts feel unmotivated.

theory_units.title: Staging Patterns & Camera Placement
theory_units.summary: Basic patterns of figure deployment (A, I, L) simplify actor arrangements according to the line of action, directly influencing optimal camera placement.
theory_units.applies_when: When initially planning actor placement and corresponding camera positions for a scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Simplifies complex staging, ensures adherence to the line of action, and guides efficient camera setup.

theory_units.title: Actor Position & Frame Composition
theory_units.summary: Within a given staging pattern, the direction actors are facing (their 'position') subtly but significantly determines the final composition of the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: After establishing a basic actor pattern and camera position, to refine the visual balance and focus within the frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Achieves precise compositional control and impacts audience interpretation of character relationships and focus.

theory_units.title: I-Pattern as Staging Building Block
theory_units.summary: The 'I' pattern, suitable for two subjects, is considered the fundamental building block for staging, as the line of action is primarily established between two individuals.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning dialogue or interaction involving two or more characters, as understanding two-person dynamics simplifies larger group staging.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a scalable and consistent framework for staging, ensuring continuity of the line of action.

theory_units.title: Profile Framing for Subject Opposition
theory_units.summary: Framing two subjects in profile, facing each other with parallel shoulders (Position One), creates strong compositional opposition.
theory_units.applies_when: When emphasizing a direct opposition or clear visual distinction between two conversing characters.
theory_units.expected_effect: Generates a sense of confrontation or clear delineation between subjects, though it limits visibility of facial expressions.
theory_units.caution: Limits visibility of detailed facial expressions unless framing is very tight.

theory_units.title: Classic OTS Shot/Reverse Shot Pattern
theory_units.summary: The over-the-shoulder (OTS) shot, reverse shot pattern is a classic technique for continuous dialogue, typically using matched pairs for consistency.
theory_units.applies_when: For dynamic and engaging continuous dialogue exchanges between two characters.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains geographic continuity and character focus, allowing for intimate portrayal of reactions.
theory_units.caution: While mixed pairs are possible, matched pairs (consistent lens and framing) are more commonplace in continuous dialogue.

theory_units.title: Isolating Subject with Foreground Block
theory_units.summary: In tight over-the-shoulder framings, blocking one-third to one-half of the frame with the foreground subject strongly isolates the background character.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to emphasize the isolation or solitary focus of the character facing the camera.
theory_units.expected_effect: Strongly directs viewer attention to the isolated subject, creating a sense of psychological distance or singular focus.

theory_units.title: Long Lens for Intimacy in OTS
theory_units.summary: Using a long focal length lens with tight framing in an OTS shot creates a more intimate feeling compared to wider lenses.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming to create a sense of close proximity, intimacy, or direct connection between the audience and the subject in an OTS shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: A more intimate and compressed perspective, bringing the viewer psychologically closer to the subject.

theory_units.title: Low Angle for Adversarial Relationship
theory_units.summary: Dynamic, low-angle reverse shots (sometimes 'over-the-hip') tend to place subjects in an adversarial relationship.
theory_units.applies_when: When portraying characters in conflict, disagreement, or a power struggle.
theory_units.expected_effect: Highlights tension and makes the subjects appear more imposing or challenging to each other, fostering a sense of confrontation.
theory_units.caution: Slightly low angles create less separation than significantly low angles.

theory_units.title: Long Lens for Background Emphasis via Focus
theory_units.summary: Increasing the focal length of the lens in an OTS can soften the focus on the foreground framing subject, thereby emphasizing the background figure.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wishes to draw primary attention to the background character in an OTS shot, rather than the foreground framing element.
theory_units.expected_effect: Shifts audience focus and empathy to the background character, potentially revealing their reactions more clearly or giving them prominence.

theory_units.title: Shot Size Affects Scene Type Perception
theory_units.summary: The chosen shot size significantly influences the audience's perception of the scene's type and dramatic context.
theory_units.applies_when: When selecting initial shot sizes for a scene, considering how the framing will immediately inform the audience about the scene's nature.
theory_units.expected_effect: Immediately establishes mood, scope, and intimacy, guiding audience expectations for the dramatic content.

theory_units.title: Caution on CUs Breaking Up Scenes
theory_units.summary: While legitimate in continuity style, using frequent close-ups can sometimes disrupt the flow and unity of a scene.
theory_units.applies_when: When considering the rhythm and pacing of editing a dialogue scene with multiple close-ups.
theory_units.expected_effect: Can heighten emotional impact but risks fragmenting the scene's spatial or emotional coherence if overused.
theory_units.caution: Over-reliance on CUs might break up the scene's overall unity, even if technically 'legitimate'.

theory_units.title: Angular CU for Audience Inclusion
theory_units.summary: Close-ups where the subject looks directly or near-directly towards the camera (the audience's direction) create a stronger sense of presence and include the viewer in the scene.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wishes to establish a direct connection between a character and the audience, making the viewer feel more involved.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances emotional connection, immediacy, and makes the audience feel like an active participant or observer within the scene.

theory_units.title: Position Three Core Staging for Casual Interactions
theory_units.summary: Position Three deploys figures at a 90-degree angle to each other, offering a more casual and less intimate pose than face-to-face or shoulder-to-shoulder.
theory_units.applies_when: When portraying relaxed, less confrontational, or non-intimate conversations, allowing characters more freedom in head positions and gaze.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys a looser relationship between characters and a more relaxed atmosphere.
theory_units.caution: Not suitable for intimate or argumentative conversations.

theory_units.title: Favored Position in Angular Two-Shot
theory_units.summary: In an angular two-shot, the player facing the camera is generally perceived to be in the favored, more prominent position.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to subtly grant more prominence or audience identification to one character in a two-shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws the viewer's attention and potential empathy more strongly to the character who is more directly facing the camera.

theory_units.title: Head-on Two-Shot for Equal Basis
theory_units.summary: A head-on two-shot places both players on an equal visual basis, making it a logical choice for a master shot without close-ups or reverses.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to show both characters as equally important or in a balanced relationship, particularly for establishing a scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys a sense of impartiality and balance between characters.
theory_units.caution: Less dynamic than setups that favor one character or allow for shot/reverse sequences.

theory_units.title: Tension from Absence of Eye Contact
theory_units.summary: Staging situations where characters avoid eye contact is a direct method to create tension in a scene.
theory_units.applies_when: When the dramatic intention is to build suspense, conflict, or portray discomfort and unresolved issues between characters.
theory_units.expected_effect: Instantly generates a feeling of unease, unresolved conflict, or emotional distance for the audience.

theory_units.title: Depth Staging for Privileged POV
theory_units.summary: Staging in depth, where one character faces away from another and towards the camera, provides the viewer with a privileged point of view, revealing reactions unseen by the other character.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to involve the audience more deeply in one character's internal experience or reactions, or to create dramatic irony.
theory_units.expected_effect: Engages the audience by making them privy to information or emotions that other characters are not, enhancing dramatic tension or empathy.
theory_units.caution: A reverse shot in this staging drastically alters the point of view; use with caution if a neutral relationship is desired.

theory_units.title: Wide Lens Effects in Depth Staging
theory_units.summary: Using a wide-angle lens (e.g., 30mm) in depth staging can create slight distortion in the foreground player and make background players appear further away.
theory_units.applies_when: When emphasizing the spatial separation between characters, or creating a slightly disorienting or exaggerated perspective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances the perception of distance and can add a subtle psychological layer through foreground distortion.
theory_units.caution: Be aware of potential distortion, especially for close foreground subjects.

theory_units.title: Wider CU/MS for Relaxed Feeling
theory_units.summary: Making a close-up wider, bordering on a medium shot, can contribute to a more relaxed feeling within the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to ease tension or create a less intense and more comfortable atmosphere in a close-up context.
theory_units.expected_effect: Softens the intensity of a close-up, providing more 'breathing room' and a less insistent or confrontational mood.

theory_units.title: Lower Angle for Less Insistent Feeling
theory_units.summary: A lower angle close-up can contribute to a sequence feeling 'less insistent', potentially reducing perceived aggression or intensity.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director desires to temper the directness or confrontational nature of a close-up, making the interaction feel softer or less demanding.
theory_units.expected_effect: Subtly reduces the intensity or confrontational edge, creating a more tempered or reflective mood.

theory_units.title: Staging for Separation and Tension
theory_units.summary: Staging that utilizes body language such as folded arms or hands in pockets, combined with a lack of eye contact, inherently creates a sense of separation and tension.
theory_units.applies_when: When portraying characters who are emotionally distant, in disagreement, or withholding information from each other.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the emotional or physical divide between characters, heightening dramatic tension through non-verbal cues.
theory_units.caution: Dominance can be established by character action within this neutral framing, e.g., one character refusing eye contact for control.

theory_units.title: High Angle for Tension and Isolation
theory_units.summary: A high-angle shot typically creates a sense of tension and isolation for the subjects within the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to make characters appear vulnerable, small, or disconnected from their environment, or to create an ominous mood.
theory_units.expected_effect: Can convey a feeling of unease, powerlessness, or detachment for the audience observing the characters.

theory_units.title: Breaking the 180-Degree Rule for Effect
theory_units.summary: Directors should not automatically discard a shot for crossing the line of action if it effectively serves the scene's purpose.
theory_units.applies_when: When conventional continuity rules like the 180-degree convention hinder a more effective or dramatic visual solution.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for greater creative freedom and potentially more impactful or unconventional visual storytelling, provided it is justified by the scene's needs.
theory_units.caution: Must be used judiciously, with a clear understanding of its effect, to avoid confusing the audience or disrupting narrative clarity.

theory_units.title: Withholding Eye Contact for Dramatic Effect
theory_units.summary: Staging where characters consistently withhold eye contact is a powerful tool to achieve specific dramatic effects.
theory_units.applies_when: When portraying emotional distance, conflict, internal struggle, or when building anticipation and dramatic tension between characters.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of mystery, unresolved conflict, or emotional weight, allowing non-verbal cues to carry significant meaning.

theory_units.title: Caution Against Overcutting
theory_units.summary: Excessive cutting within a scene, especially with certain in-depth stagings, can destroy the scene's unity.
theory_units.applies_when: When editing scenes that rely on sustained shots or in-depth staging for their dramatic impact.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains the scene's flow and spatial coherence, allowing the audience to engage with the unfolding action and character dynamics without interruption.
theory_units.caution: Overcutting can fragment the narrative, confuse spatial relationships, and diminish the emotional impact of carefully composed longer shots.

theory_units.title: In-depth Staging for Foreground Identification
theory_units.summary: In-depth staging, particularly when one character is positioned prominently in the foreground, encourages the audience to identify with that foreground player.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to create a strong emotional connection or empathy between the audience and a specific character.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws the audience into the foreground character's perspective, fostering a sense of intimacy and subjective experience.

theory_units.title: Offscreen Gaze for Divided Attention & Relaxed Mood
theory_units.summary: When both players look offscreen in different directions, viewer attention is divided, creating an offhanded, relaxed dramatic situation.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming for a casual, non-confrontational, or contemplative mood where characters are not intensely focused on each other.
theory_units.expected_effect: Generates a relaxed atmosphere, suggesting a natural or less intense interaction, and allows the audience to observe rather than be directly engaged.

theory_units.title: Background Gaze for Shot Unification
theory_units.summary: If a background player looks past the foreground player towards something specific, it unifies the shot by directing the viewer's attention to the foreground player.
theory_units.applies_when: When staging two characters in depth, and the director wants to subtly guide the viewer's eye and create a cohesive visual connection between them.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents the viewer's attention from being completely divided, instead channeling it through the background player's gaze to the foreground subject, unifying the composition.

theory_units.title: Player Dominance by Eye Clarity
theory_units.summary: As a general rule, the player whose eyes are most clearly visible and prominent in the shot will tend to dominate the shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When strategically assigning visual weight or importance to one character over another within a single frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Directs audience focus and emotional connection to the dominant character, influencing perceptions of power or narrative importance.

theory_units.title: Angular Shots for Balanced Attention
theory_units.summary: Angular shots where both players are turned away from the camera can balance the attention given to each figure, preventing one from dominating the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to portray characters as equally important, or to avoid favoring one character's perspective in a multi-person shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a visual equilibrium between subjects, promoting a more objective or balanced view for the audience.

theory_units.title: Explore Relationships with Reverse Shots
theory_units.summary: Use a pair of reverse shots to more fully explore the relationship between characters.
theory_units.applies_when: When you want to delve deeper into the connection or dynamic between two characters.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances audience understanding of character relationships and their interaction.

theory_units.title: In-Depth Staging (Frontality Focus)
theory_units.summary: Design staging in depth using frontality to work effectively without needing reverse shots or shots taken from the side.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming for a scene flow that emphasizes frontality and minimizes cuts, avoiding reverses or side angles.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains a direct, frontal perspective; creates a unique visual flow without traditional continuity cuts.

theory_units.title: Cut on the Look for Intrigue (Non-POV)
theory_units.summary: Cut from a character's look to a wider frame of what they are observing to create intrigue, which is distinct from a subjective POV shot requiring a reverse angle.
theory_units.applies_when: To build initial intrigue or establish scene space from a character's perspective without fully committing to a POV.
theory_units.expected_effect: Generates curiosity in the audience; clearly establishes the object of a character's attention.
theory_units.caution: Understand that this is not a POV shot and does not require a reverse angle to maintain spatial logic.

theory_units.title: Wide Establishing Shot for Pause/Finality
theory_units.summary: Use a wide establishing shot to serve as a dramatic pause in the middle of a scene or as its final shot, providing a sense of completion or reflection.
theory_units.applies_when: To create a moment of reflection, transition, or to signify the conclusion of a scene or sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dramatic beat or pause; provides a definitive sense of ending or transition.

theory_units.title: A-Pattern Staging with Varied Heights
theory_units.summary: When using an A-pattern arrangement, stage players at different heights to achieve more interesting and dynamic camera angles.
theory_units.applies_when: When setting up an A-pattern and desiring to break up monotony or add visual interest to the composition.
theory_units.expected_effect: More dynamic and visually engaging angles; emphasizes different characters within the group.

theory_units.title: Unorthodox Line of Action
theory_units.summary: Establish the line of action in an unconventional manner, not strictly basing it on the sight lines of the players, to explore new staging possibilities.
theory_units.applies_when: When seeking to deliberately challenge or experiment with traditional spatial continuity for a specific aesthetic or dramatic effect.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates an unconventional or dynamic sense of space; allows for new camera positions.
theory_units.caution: This rule-breaking approach is a directorial decision and may not work for all scenes or audiences.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Scene Geography with Spatial Signposts
theory_units.summary: Ensure scene geography is clearly established early on and include deliberate spatial signposts (e.g., props) to allow for radical shifts in camera angle or line crossing without disorienting the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning complex camera movements, radical angle shifts, or intentional violations of the line of action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience maintains understanding of spatial relationships despite unconventional camera work; enables bold directorial choices.

theory_units.title: Using Spatial Cues for Cohesive Editing (Line Crossing)
theory_units.summary: Incorporate head turns, eye lines, and other spatial cues to make editing patterns more cohesive, especially when the line of action is crossed or camera positions are unconventional.
theory_units.applies_when: When editing sequences that involve complex blocking, multiple lines of action, or intentional rule-breaking, to help guide the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increases editing cohesion and audience understanding of spatial relationships, even with challenging camera work.

theory_units.title: Action or Look as Cut Motivator
theory_units.summary: Motivate cuts between shots by a character's action or their 'look' (eye line) to ensure a natural and cohesive flow in the editing.
theory_units.applies_when: General principle for editing any scene, especially dialogue or reaction sequences, to maintain audience engagement and clarity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamless, logical, and audience-engaging editing that feels natural.

theory_units.title: Consolidation & Simplification for Large Groups
theory_units.summary: When staging scenes with four or more subjects, prioritize consolidation and simplification of shot choices to manage the overwhelming number of possibilities.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing dialogue scenes or interactions involving four or more characters.
theory_units.expected_effect: Manages complexity, keeps the focus clear, and prevents an overwhelming number of camera setups.

theory_units.title: Focus on Key Characters in Large Groups
theory_units.summary: In scenes involving large numbers of people, focus the camera and dramatic attention on the key experiences of the main characters within a compressed timeframe.
theory_units.applies_when: When staging any scene with many background characters, ensuring the narrative remains centered on the protagonists.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains dramatic clarity and narrative focus, preventing the story from becoming diluted by too many subjects.

theory_units.title: Use Close-Ups to Differentiate Speakers in Large Groups
theory_units.summary: When multiple characters speak in a large group setting, frequently use close-ups over three- or four-player group shots to clearly differentiate the individual speakers.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing dialogue in scenes with large ensembles where several characters have speaking parts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Helps the audience identify and follow individual speakers, enhancing clarity and engagement.

theory_units.title: Identify Central Players for Camera Positioning
theory_units.summary: The primary determinant for camera positioning in group scenes is identifying which players are the central, most dramatically significant characters.
theory_units.applies_when: Initial planning of camera setups for any scene involving multiple characters.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures optimal camera placement that aligns with the dramatic focus of the scene and highlights key performances.

theory_units.title: Preserve Line of Action for Principal Players
theory_units.summary: When staging large groups, establish the line of action between the principal two players and preserve it, even when using close-ups of other characters.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing scenes with multiple characters where a core interaction needs to maintain spatial continuity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains spatial clarity and continuity for the audience, especially for the central dramatic interaction.

theory_units.title: 180-Degree Rule for Non-Speaking Players
theory_units.summary: When including non-speaking players in a shot, restrict camera position to the 180-degree working area defined by the line of action of the speaking players.
theory_units.applies_when: Composing shots in dialogue scenes, especially when background or secondary characters are visible but not actively participating in the dialogue.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains spatial continuity for the audience and avoids disorientation.

theory_units.title: Limit Key Setups/Sightlines in Large Groups
theory_units.summary: To simplify staging and avoid unnecessary problems in large groups, limit yourself to a few key setups and aim for no more than four active sightlines.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning scenes with four or more key players and potentially complex interactions or multiple lines of action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Reduces staging complexity, maintains clarity, and prevents overwhelming the audience or crew.
theory_units.caution: Establishing more than four sightlines can create unnecessary problems.

theory_units.title: General Viewing Direction via Basic Line of Action
theory_units.summary: Establish a basic line of action in large groups to define a general viewing direction, which allows for various shot types (CUs, singles, two-shots, group shots) within that consistent orientation.
theory_units.applies_when: Staging large group scenes with multiple potential lines of action to create a cohesive shooting strategy.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a clear organizational principle for camera placement, maintains spatial continuity, and simplifies shot selection.

theory_units.title: Single Camera Setup for Continuity Simplicity
theory_units.summary: Using a single camera setup for large group stagings can eliminate continuity problems, albeit potentially at the expense of dynamic cutting.
theory_units.applies_when: When prioritizing absolute continuity and simplicity in staging large group scenes, or when a more static, observational style is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Completely eliminates continuity errors, provides a clear and consistent viewpoint for the entire scene.
theory_units.caution: May result in a less dynamic or active cutting style.

theory_units.title: Line of Action for Determining Camera Geography
theory_units.summary: Regardless of staging complexity, the camera geography of any scene can be easily determined by always keeping the line of action in mind.
theory_units.applies_when: Any stage of scene planning and execution, from blocking to camera setup.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a clear and consistent framework for camera placement, ensuring spatial logic and preventing disorientation.
theory_units.caution: This is true whether you choose to observe or violate the line of action.

theory_units.title: Line of Action as Organizational System
theory_units.summary: The line of action and its derived patterns should be conceptualized as a system of organization for scene space and camera placement, rather than a fixed aesthetic choice.
theory_units.applies_when: When approaching scene blocking and camera coverage, allowing for deliberate deviation once the system is understood.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a practical, logical framework for decision-making; empowers directors to break rules meaningfully.

theory_units.title: Flexible Interpretation of Staging Patterns
theory_units.summary: In circular or complex character arrangements, the staging can be flexibly interpreted as I, A, or L patterns depending on which players are being emphasized, leaving the determination of the line of action and viewing angle to the director's choice.
theory_units.applies_when: Staging complex or circular group dynamics where the focus might shift between different subsets of characters.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for directorial flexibility in defining focus and continuity within complex arrangements.

theory_units.title: Predominant OTS Angle for Circular Staging
theory_units.summary: In circular staging, establish a predominant over-the-shoulder (OTS) viewing angle from a key character, which can allow all other players to be viewed from this position, requiring only one reverse shot to see the key character.
theory_units.applies_when: Staging scenes with characters arranged in a circular formation where a central figure acts as a viewing anchor.
theory_units.expected_effect: Efficient camera coverage, clear spatial relationships, and reduced number of necessary reverse shots.

theory_units.title: Flexible Line of Action in Circular Staging
theory_units.summary: Circular staging inherently offers an extremely flexible line of action due to the multitude of possible sight lines, allowing a director to easily establish a new line anywhere in the scene space.
theory_units.applies_when: Staging circular group dynamics where a director needs the freedom to shift focus and spatial orientation dynamically.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides significant adaptability in staging, allowing for dynamic changes in character emphasis and camera placement.

theory_units.title: Treating Paired Characters as a Single Unit
theory_units.summary: When two characters are seated side-by-side and function as a central unit, they can be framed and treated as if they were a single 'player' for staging purposes, effectively simplifying to an I-pattern interaction.
theory_units.applies_when: Staging scenes where two characters naturally form a cohesive visual and dramatic unit.
theory_units.expected_effect: Simplifies complex staging to a more manageable two-subject pattern, maintaining focus on the pair.

theory_units.title: Master Shot Framing with Mixed Angles
theory_units.summary: A single master shot can effectively frame multiple characters by adjusting camera position and tilt, potentially capturing seated figures in profile and standing figures frontally within the same frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When designing a master shot to cover an entire group and needing to incorporate varied character positions and angles.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides comprehensive coverage in one shot while allowing for varied and dynamic character presentation within the frame.

theory_units.title: Mixing Staging Patterns
theory_units.summary: Different staging patterns (I, L, A) can be comfortably mixed within a sequence, with the ultimate choice often depending on whether symmetrical or asymmetrical framing is desired.
theory_units.applies_when: Designing complex shot sequences with multiple characters, allowing for varied dynamics and aesthetic choices across the sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Offers flexible and dynamic shot design, enabling a director to achieve a wide range of visual styles and emphasis.

theory_units.title: Master Shot for Dramatically Significant Mid-Sized Groups
theory_units.summary: Master shot stagings are frequently desirable for mid-sized groups (e.g., three to five players) where each subject holds significant dramatic importance.
theory_units.applies_when: When directing scenes with a small to medium number of key characters who all contribute significantly to the scene's drama.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the group dynamic and ensures all dramatically significant characters are prominently featured.

theory_units.title: Staging Along Lens Axis in Group Master Shots
theory_units.summary: To prevent a group master shot from appearing like a flat, theatrical proscenium, stage players along the lens axis (in depth) rather than spread across the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: Composing group master shots where a more cinematic sense of depth and realism is desired, rather than a flat, stage-like presentation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates cinematic depth and dimension; avoids a 'staginess' or flat, tableau effect.

theory_units.title: Foreground Player Action in Depth Staging
theory_units.summary: In in-depth staging, direct foreground players to dynamically interact by turning to react to background players or speaking/responding to players across from them, preventing a static foreground.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing dialogue or reactions in scenes where players are staged along the lens axis, utilizing foreground elements.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates dynamic interactions, maintains visual interest in the foreground, and enhances the sense of depth within the scene.

theory_units.title: Loosening Background Groups in In-Depth Compositions
theory_units.summary: When using in-depth composition with a foreground player, modify overly composed background groups into looser arrangements to achieve a more naturalistic look and avoid a theatrical feeling.
theory_units.applies_when: Refining in-depth compositions that include multiple background characters, aiming for a less stiff or artificial appearance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Results in a more natural, less 'posed' aesthetic; reduces the risk of staginess.

theory_units.title: Disregard Ordered Framing to Avoid Staginess
theory_units.summary: To cure staginess caused by overcomposed figures in group shots, directors should disregard overly ordered or perfectly neat framing.
theory_units.applies_when: Composing group shots where characters appear too 'placed' or artificial due to a fear of not being clearly seen.
theory_units.expected_effect: Achieves a more natural and less theatrical appearance for group interactions.
theory_units.caution: Filmmakers' fear that players are not seen clearly can lead to overcomposition.

theory_units.title: Open Framing for Staging Freedom
theory_units.summary: Utilize 'open framing,' where figures are overlapped or intentionally cut off by the frame, to increase staging options and directorial freedom.
theory_units.applies_when: Seeking greater flexibility and dynamism in staging action and composing shots, moving away from rigid, centered framing.
theory_units.expected_effect: More dynamic and realistic composition; significantly expands possibilities for character placement and interaction within the frame.

theory_units.title: Crowd Dialogue Camera Position
theory_units.summary: When shooting dialogue in or around a crowd, position the camera either inside the crowd looking out, or outside the crowd looking in.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming dialogue in scenes densely packed with people.
theory_units.expected_effect: Organizes the fundamental camera strategy for complex crowd scenes, addressing spatial problems.

theory_units.title: Lens Choice for Crowd Perspective
theory_units.summary: The choice of lens focal length dictates the camera's relationship to the crowd: wide/normal lenses for 'in-action' shots, and telephoto lenses for 'outside-action' shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Deciding on the appropriate lens for crowd scenes based on the desired camera's perspective relative to the action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Achieves the intended immersive (inside) or observational (outside) perspective of the crowd scene.

theory_units.title: Telephoto for Crowd Simulation & Isolation
theory_units.summary: Telephoto lenses can simulate large masses of people with a limited number of extras staged in depth, and due to their shallow depth of field, they can isolate principal subjects from background and foreground crowd elements.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to create the appearance of a large crowd with limited resources, or to highlight and separate principal subjects within a dense crowd.
theory_units.expected_effect: Efficiently creates the illusion of a large crowd and enhances focus on main subjects, regardless of crowd authenticity.
theory_units.caution: Spatial relationships within shots become indefinite, and the specific location of action is difficult to identify due to shallow depth of field.

theory_units.title: Telephoto for Discrete Filming in Crowds
theory_units.summary: Telephoto lenses allow the camera to be placed at a distance from the crowd, making it easier for the cameraman to work discretely and photograph actors in real or staged crowd situations.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming in real crowd environments where camera discretion is important, or when crew proximity to subjects is a logistical challenge.
theory_units.expected_effect: Facilitates easier camera operation, allows for more natural actor interaction by reducing crew visibility, and enables discrete capture of performances.

theory_units.title: Telephoto Crowd Staging Rule
theory_units.summary: For telephoto shots of subjects within a crowd, the camera must be placed outside the action, and extras must be carefully staged so that only a few people move between the camera and principal subjects, making a small group seem like a large crowd.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning telephoto shots where subjects are intended to appear embedded within a large crowd.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents subjects from being obscured by too many foreground extras while maintaining the illusion of a dense crowd, maximizing the impact of limited extras.
theory_units.caution: If the camera is in the midst of the crowd, it risks too many extras obscuring the players; requires careful staging.

theory_units.title: Challenges of Wide Lenses in Crowds
theory_units.summary: Staging action for a wide lens in a crowd is difficult because the camera is close to the subject, the greater depth of field and clarity are less forgiving, and subject/camera movement requires significantly more extras to fill the wider frame.
theory_units.applies_when: Considering using wide or normal lenses for action sequences within a dense crowd.
theory_units.expected_effect: Highlights the increased logistical and staging complexities, emphasizing the need for extremely precise figure positioning and a larger number of extras.
theory_units.caution: Extremely precise positioning of figures is critical; a slight variation can ruin the shot. Requires clearing areas for crew and equipment movement.

theory_units.title: Lens Application for Crowd Action vs. Dialogue
theory_units.summary: Wider lenses are generally necessary for staging physical action and creating understandable geography in crowd scenes, while telephoto lenses are better suited for dialogue stagings within a crowd.
theory_units.applies_when: Deciding on lens type based on the primary focus of a crowd scene (physical action/location vs. dialogue).
theory_units.expected_effect: Optimizes lens choice for clarity of either physical action and spatial relationships or focused dialogue delivery within a crowd context.

theory_units.title: Fundamental Mobile Staging Methods
theory_units.summary: The two basic methods of staging mobile action are to either move the camera (e.g., tracking, crane shots) or move the subjects within the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning any scene that involves dynamic movement, whether from actors or the camera.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a fundamental framework for conceiving and choreographing movement, offering flexibility in directing viewer attention.

theory_units.title: Combining Staging Approaches
theory_units.summary: To create varied and fluid dramatic sequences, directors frequently combine cutting between multiple camera viewpoints with moving the subject within the frame and moving the camera itself (tracking or crane shots).
theory_units.applies_when: Designing complex, dynamic sequences that require varied visual rhythm and continuous engagement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Produces a more dynamic, varied, and fluid dramatic sequence by integrating all available staging and photographic techniques.

theory_units.title: Actor Movement for Editing Efficiency
theory_units.summary: Actors can reposition themselves within a single, continuous shot to achieve the same results as cutting between setups, effectively generating different angles, shot sizes, or perspectives without resorting to editing.
theory_units.applies_when: Desiring to avoid cuts, maintain unbroken continuity, or emphasize actor performance within a single take for a fluid dramatic effect.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates the impression of multiple shots within one continuous take, enhancing realism and dramatic tension by preserving a unified space and time.
theory_units.caution: Actor movement must be motivated and naturalistic (stage business) to avoid seeming artificial.

theory_units.title: Motivated Actor Movement (Stage Business)
theory_units.summary: All actor movement introduced for staging purposes, known as 'stage business,' must be motivated by the story, character, or situation, rather than being invented artificially to simply add action.
theory_units.applies_when: Choreographing any actor movements within a scene, especially when utilizing mobile staging to achieve different framings or emphasis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures movements feel organic, contribute to the narrative or characterization, and enhance the scene's authenticity.
theory_units.caution: Never invent artificial 'business' just to add action; ideas should emerge from collaboration and observations of human behavior.

theory_units.title: Counter Move Staging
theory_units.summary: A 'counter move' is a staging technique where a subject moves in the opposite direction of the camera's movement within a single unbroken shot, often used to fluidly reframe or reveal other subjects.
theory_units.applies_when: Seeking to smoothly transition between framings or re-establish a two-shot fluidly within a single take, especially when a subject needs to pass the camera.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic, seamless shift in focus or reframing of subjects, maintaining continuity and potentially increasing dramatic emphasis within a continuous shot.
theory_units.caution: Timing and positioning are crucial for achieving the desired dramatic emphasis and ensuring subjects are not out of frame for too long.

theory_units.title: Integrated Camera & Actor Choreography for Sequence Shots
theory_units.summary: Ambitious sequence shots can integrate various techniques such as staging in depth, panning from a stationary position, retracking over the same space, following multiple subjects, and pushing in/backing away with the camera to maximize the dynamic use of a single shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Designing complex, continuous shots that cover multiple dramatic beats and require dynamic visual changes and evolving compositions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a highly fluid, engaging, and dynamic visual narrative within a single take, showcasing complex staging and integrated performance, and maximizing visual information from a limited setup.
theory_units.caution: Requires extensive rehearsal and precise coordination between camera operator, actors, and other crew members for successful execution.

theory_units.title: Collaborative On-Set Staging
theory_units.summary: Visualizing and executing scene staging requires close collaboration between the director, cast, cinematographer, and crew, with the subtleties of camera timing and the transfer of attention worked out and refined on set during rehearsal.
theory_units.applies_when: Any scene involving complex camera movement or actor blocking, especially continuous takes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Achieves precise and nuanced staging that cannot be fully anticipated in storyboards, leading to more fluid and impactful scene execution.
theory_units.caution: Requires precise communication between the director and cinematographer; the camera operator holds critical responsibilities for the speed, timing of camera moves, and the transfer of attention between actors.

theory_units.title: Importance of Reaction Shots
theory_units.summary: Reaction shots are as informative as action shots in a conversation, meaning the person speaking does not always need to be the center of attention, which can loosen up traditional staging conventions.
theory_units.applies_when: Staging dialogue scenes, particularly when seeking to add depth, build suspense, reveal subtext, or provide alternative focal points.
theory_units.expected_effect: Loosens rigid staging rules, provides insight into a character's internal state, and can make the audience more actively engaged in interpreting the scene's emotional dynamics.
theory_units.caution: Filmmakers are frequently over-concerned with focusing solely on the 'action' (the person speaking).

theory_units.title: Varied Visuals for Reaction Shots
theory_units.summary: Reaction shots are not limited to close-ups of a character's face; they can include specific body language (hands, feet) or even point-of-view shots of objects/environments to convey a character's feelings or understanding.
theory_units.applies_when: Crafting impactful and nuanced reaction shots that go beyond conventional facial expressions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Expands the expressive range of reaction shots, provides deeper insight into character psychology, and avoids visual monotony by utilizing diverse visual cues.

theory_units.title: Moving Center of Interest Strategy
theory_units.summary: The camera can follow a subject who is the 'center of interest' as they move around other stationary players, thereby directing the viewer's attention to the reactions of those other players, all within a single continuous shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Designing scenes where one character's actions or dialogue significantly influence others, and where multiple reactions need to be captured dynamically and simultaneously.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a highly dynamic and informative single shot that captures both the central action and multiple peripheral reactions, maintaining fluidity and emphasizing the central figure's impact.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful execution and precise camera operation to ensure reactions are clearly visible and compositions remain effective throughout the movement.

theory_units.title: Indirection and Selective Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Not every story point or line of dialogue in a scene needs to be overtly emphasized; selectively holding back expressive power through indirection (e.g., relegating action to the background) can make truly important moments stand out more.
theory_units.applies_when: Deciding how to visually present information or dialogue, aiming for nuanced and sophisticated storytelling.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents visual fatigue, makes moments of true significance more impactful, and can add subtlety and realism to the narrative.
theory_units.caution: Avoid the common misconception that an important line of dialogue always requires a close-up or full-screen composition.

theory_units.title: Emphasizing Subtlety
theory_units.summary: Sometimes the smallest gesture is the most telling, and people are often most attentive to those who speak softly, freeing the filmmaker from feeling compelled to compose every dramatic point full screen.
theory_units.applies_when: Deciding on framing and emphasis for moments of emotional or narrative significance, particularly in dialogue-heavy scenes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for more naturalistic and nuanced performances to convey deep meaning, avoids over-dramatization, and enhances audience engagement with subtle cues.

theory_units.title: Camera 'In the Action' Staging
theory_units.summary: Positioning the camera within the 'dramatic circle of action' (the space actors cover) to immerse the viewer.
theory_units.applies_when: To heighten viewer identification with a character's journey, or to emphasize a character's movement and changing prominence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased viewer identification with the character; character's size and prominence in the frame will vary significantly; the action will have a clear beginning, middle, and end, like a self-contained drama.
theory_units.caution: Requires extensive camera movement (e.g., panning up to 180 degrees) to cover a single continuous movement.

theory_units.title: Camera 'Out of the Action' Staging
theory_units.summary: Positioning the camera outside the 'dramatic circle of action' (the space actors cover) to offer a more objective view.
theory_units.applies_when: To achieve a distanced or neutral observation of the action, to cover an entire movement without significant camera movement, or to maintain consistent character size in the frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Distanced and neutral viewer observation; character's size in frame remains relatively constant throughout the shot; can cover the entire movement with little or no panning (especially with a sufficiently wide-angle lens).

theory_units.title: Deep Staging to Minimize Cutting
theory_units.summary: Arranging subjects at various depths within a single shot to eliminate or reduce the need for editing.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming for continuous action, a unified visual field, or to allow selective emphasis of dramatic elements within one frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Reduced or eliminated cuts, creating a unified and continuous visual experience; ability to create graphic oppositions within the frame; attention can be shifted to near or far players by using lighting, depth of field, narrative context, or mobile staging.

theory_units.title: Deep Staging for Emotional Separation (Welles Style)
theory_units.summary: Utilizing extensive depth to spatially separate characters, often placing them in foreground and background spaces, to convey emotional or psychological isolation.
theory_units.applies_when: To visually represent character estrangement, isolation, or power imbalances within a scene, making characters appear 'imprisoned spatially'.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience perceives characters as emotionally or psychologically separated despite being in the same frame.

theory_units.title: Deep Staging for Narrative Flow (Renoir Style)
theory_units.summary: Moving actors from foreground to background within a single shot to guide viewer attention and introduce new stages of the story.
theory_units.applies_when: To introduce new narrative elements or shift viewer focus smoothly from one point of interest to another within a single, continuous take, eliminating cuts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamless narrative progression; continuous viewer attention guided through space; a sense of unfolding events within a single take.

theory_units.title: Linking Ideas Through Spatial Depth
theory_units.summary: Placing symbolically or thematically related objects or elements at different depths within the frame to create conceptual connections.
theory_units.applies_when: To add layers of meaning, foreshadowing, or metaphorical commentary to a shot without explicit dialogue or action, or to define distinct areas of meaning within the frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates implicit conceptual links and deeper thematic resonance for the audience, enhancing the shot's subtextual meaning.

theory_units.title: Using Split-Field Diopter Lenses
theory_units.summary: A technique using a partial close-up lens attachment to achieve simultaneous sharp focus on extreme foreground and background elements within a single shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When deep focus is desired for elements at extreme foreground and background distances within a static shot, and traditional deep focus with a wide-angle lens is not feasible.
theory_units.expected_effect: Both very near and very far subjects appear in sharp focus within the same frame, creating a unique deep-focus composition.
theory_units.caution: A visible blur line exists where the diopter ends; this line *must* be concealed through artful composition of all elements in the shot. The camera *must* be locked off (static), and no person or object *must* move across the split line during the shot. Foreground and background elements are restricted to one half of the frame.

theory_units.title: Compressed Depth with Telephoto Lenses
theory_units.summary: Using telephoto lenses to flatten the visual depth of the frame, emphasizing width and making distant elements appear closer together.
theory_units.applies_when: To create a specific aesthetic (e.g., muted, dreamy), emphasize lateral separation between subjects, simplify continuity challenges, or make backgrounds appear larger and more prominent.
theory_units.expected_effect: Flattened scene perspective where subjects appear closer to each other than they are in reality; backgrounds are magnified and prominent; can create a 'muted and dreamy' visual style (Altman) or emphasize the 'width of the scene space'. Simplifies continuity blocking.
theory_units.caution: Makes differentiation between staging patterns more difficult unless separation of players is lateral. Mobile staging (in depth) is problematic as subjects repositioning in depth will appear to move without arriving at a new space. Camera movement in depth will appear negligible.

theory_units.title: Viewer Transference from Camera Movement/Angle
theory_units.summary: The viewer identifies with the camera; camera movement (tracking, cutting) or changes in viewing angle create a sensation of physical movement and make the images feel more real, a phenomenon called transference. Varying viewing angles specifically contribute to this physical excitement.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming to physically engage the audience and make the on-screen action feel more immediate and real.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased viewer identification with the camera, physical excitement, enhanced realism, deeper immersion.

theory_units.title: Evocative Camera Angles in Confined Spaces
theory_units.summary: Judiciously chosen camera angles can make a cramped space as emotionally resonant and evocative as a vast one, without requiring elaborate camera moves or wide vistas.
theory_units.applies_when: When shooting in confined or small locations, or when aiming for a strong emotional or thematic impact within limited physical space.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhanced emotional depth and resonance of the scene, regardless of the physical size of the set.

theory_units.title: Sequential Perspective for Cinematic Choreography
theory_units.summary: Placing two shots side-by-side creates a new spatial experience ('sequential perspective'), allowing the filmmaker to choreograph the viewer's journey through the screen space and design effective shot flow.
theory_units.applies_when: When designing the sequence of shots to guide the viewer's spatial understanding and emotional experience.
theory_units.expected_effect: A dynamic and engaging spatial experience for the viewer, making them an active participant in the scene's visual rhythm.

theory_units.title: Eye-Level View for Stability and Contrast
theory_units.summary: Straight-on eye-level views inherently create a sense of stability, making them suitable for establishing a baseline or providing contrast to more dynamic compositions.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to convey calm, normalcy, or a stable point of reference, or to set up a visual contrast with more energetic shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: A feeling of groundedness, neutrality, or visual calm; can heighten the impact of subsequent dynamic shots.
theory_units.caution: Overuse might lead to a lack of dynamism unless intentionally used for a specific monotonous effect.

theory_units.title: Progressive Shot Flow (Depth and Tightening)
theory_units.summary: A progressive shot flow creates a sense of forward motion by gradually increasing the degree of perspective (more receding planes visible) and tightening the shots within a sequence.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to guide the viewer smoothly through space, create a build-up of tension, or convey a clear sense of progress and advancement within a sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: A smooth, continuous sense of forward motion and spatial progression, drawing the viewer deeper into the scene.

theory_units.title: Nonprogressive Shot Flow (Angular Conflict)
theory_units.summary: A nonprogressive shot flow is characterized by conflicting angular views between successive frames, creating a sense of discontinuity or disruption rather than smooth progression.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to create a jarring effect, disorient the viewer, or emphasize conflict and tension through visual means.
theory_units.expected_effect: A sense of visual tension, conflict, or disjointedness, breaking the smooth flow of perception.
theory_units.caution: Can disorient or confuse the audience if not used purposefully.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Low-Angle Views
theory_units.summary: Low-angle views introduce dynamism and can create visual conflict, especially when contrasted with less dynamic angles like eye-level views, making them far more dynamic.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to emphasize power, importance, or to create a more energetic and visually engaging composition. Also useful for creating deliberate conflict in a sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased visual energy, a sense of drama or significance, and potential for conflict or tension.
theory_units.caution: Can sometimes distort proportions or make subjects appear larger than life, which may not always be desired.

theory_units.title: Location-First Storyboarding/Composition
theory_units.summary: When devising sequences, consider framing shots based on the location or background first, as changes in viewpoint and background composition subtly influence mood, pacing, and narrative events, before integrating the subject.
theory_units.applies_when: During the early stages of planning a sequence, especially when the environment plays a significant role, to discover fresh ideas for visual storytelling.
theory_units.expected_effect: A more thoughtful and integrated use of space, leading to nuanced changes in mood and pacing; new creative solutions for framing.
theory_units.caution: The subject will ultimately be a determining factor, so this is a starting point, not the final decision.

theory_units.title: Longer Lenses for Cramped Interior Realism
theory_units.summary: In cramped interiors where wide-angle perspective is dictated by room size rather than design, using longer lenses and shooting through doorways, windows, or past foreground objects can provide more artistic and less cliché compositions.
theory_units.applies_when: When shooting in real, confined interior locations where wide-angle lenses might create unflattering distortion or a generic 'TV look' due to practical constraints.
theory_units.expected_effect: More naturalistic perspective, less distortion, and visually richer compositions that avoid common wide-angle interior clichés.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful staging and potentially more complex camera setups to achieve desired framing.

theory_units.title: Vigorous Angles for Stylized/Humorous Treatment
theory_units.summary: A humorous or stylized treatment of a narrative encourages the use of more vigorous camera angles to enhance the intended tone and aesthetic.
theory_units.applies_when: When the film's tone is overtly humorous, exaggerated, or intentionally stylized, to match the visual language with the narrative's approach.
theory_units.expected_effect: Amplification of the humorous or stylized tone, making the visual language consistent with the narrative's expressive qualities.

theory_units.title: Slow Motion for Dramatic Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Employing slow motion during key moments in an action sequence can heighten drama and emphasize the significance of the event.
theory_units.applies_when: When a specific action or moment needs to be dramatically underscored, giving the audience more time to process its impact or significance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased dramatic tension, visual impact, and emphasis on the highlighted action.
theory_units.caution: Overuse can diminish its impact or slow down pacing unnecessarily.

theory_units.title: Return to Normal Speed for Impact
theory_units.summary: After a period of slow motion, returning to normal camera speed for a crucial moment can provide a sudden burst of energy and impact, delivering the climax of an action.
theory_units.applies_when: Following a slow-motion sequence, to deliver a climactic action or emphasize a critical narrative beat with full force.
theory_units.expected_effect: A jolt of energy and increased intensity, making the action feel more immediate and powerful.

theory_units.title: Pan Shot for Tracking Moving Objects
theory_units.summary: Using a pan shot is effective for following the trajectory of a fast-moving object, establishing its movement through space and its interaction with the environment.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director needs to maintain focus on a moving subject and convey its path, speed, and interaction within the scene's environment.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clear depiction of object movement, continuity of action, and engagement of the viewer in the object's journey.
theory_units.caution: Poorly executed pans can be jarring or shaky.

theory_units.title: Establishing Rhythm with Slight Camera Angle Variations
theory_units.summary: Small, subtle changes in camera angle are as crucial as extreme angles in establishing and varying the rhythm of movement within a scene.
theory_units.applies_when: When establishing or varying the rhythm of movement within a scene, especially when a continuous flow or subtle dynamism is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of visual rhythm and dynamism, contributing to the scene's overall pacing and flow.

theory_units.title: Open Framing for Realism and Viewer Immersion
theory_units.summary: Open framings are compositions where elements may be partially cut off by the frame edge or obscured by foreground, mimicking documentary style and making the scene feel less controlled and more realistic.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming for a realistic, less staged feel, or to include the viewer in the picture space by suggesting a larger world beyond the frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances realism and authenticity, making the viewer feel like an observer within a larger, uncontrolled environment, which can increase immersion.
theory_units.caution: Can be carefully arranged to look unarranged, potentially deceiving the viewer about objectivity and spontaneous reporting.

theory_units.title: Closed Framing for Clarity and Graphic Balance
theory_units.summary: Closed framings are compositions with subjects meticulously positioned for maximum clarity and graphic balance, often placing the camera outside the immediate circle of action.
theory_units.applies_when: When prioritizing clear, balanced composition, creating a formal or constructed aesthetic, or when the camera is observing from a detached position.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of order, precision, and can make the scene appear more formal, constructed, or theatrical, reducing perceived realism.
theory_units.caution: Can appear staged, potentially reducing the sense of spontaneity or realism.

theory_units.title: Manipulating Aesthetic Distance with Shot Size
theory_units.summary: The chosen shot size, from an extreme close-up to a long shot, establishes a physical relationship between the audience and the subject, which has profound psychological and moral implications.
theory_units.applies_when: When defining the viewer's emotional and physical proximity to characters or events, and controlling their level of engagement or reflection.
theory_units.expected_effect: Controls the degree of viewer manipulation and involvement, allowing for greater opportunity for reflection (long shots) or direct participation (close-ups).

theory_units.title: Composing Shots to Maintain Point of View
theory_units.summary: To effectively convey a specific character's point of view, the filmmaker must compose shots from that character's perspective or position within the scene.
theory_units.applies_when: When a scene is written from a particular character's perspective and the filmmaker wishes to visually reinforce that viewpoint for the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Encourages viewer identification and empathy with the designated character, immersing them in that character's experience.

theory_units.title: Low Angle for Viewer Identification
theory_units.summary: Placing the camera at a low angle to a character can make them easier to see and more prominent, thereby encouraging viewer identification with that character.
theory_units.applies_when: When trying to encourage the audience to identify with a particular character, especially when seen from another character's perspective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Fosters stronger viewer identification and potentially empathy with the subject, making their perspective more accessible.

theory_units.title: Strategic Shot Size Variation for Dramatic Impact
theory_units.summary: Ensuring a significant change in shot size from an opening wide shot to subsequent closer framings creates a strong visual contrast and impactful progression.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning a sequence that progresses from a wider view to more intimate close-ups, to maximize the visual and emotional impact of the transition.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances the dramatic impact of moving closer, making the close-ups feel more significant, intimate, or revealing.

theory_units.title: Using Depth of Field for Selective Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Depth of field can selectively emphasize subjects, not always by keeping them in sharp focus; an unfocused player can also be made the key subject through careful framing and action.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director wants to draw attention to a specific subject, whether by sharpness or by contrasting it with a sharp foreground/background element.
theory_units.expected_effect: Guides the viewer's eye, controls dramatic emphasis within the frame, and can reveal subtle narrative layers.
theory_units.caution: While traditionally focused subjects are emphasized, an unfocused subject can become key if framed and acted in a way that draws attention to its ambiguity or concealment.

theory_units.title: Pacing Intimacy through Shot Size Progression
theory_units.summary: Gradually moving into closer shots over a sequence allows the filmmaker to control the pace at which intimacy is introduced to the viewer, avoiding premature closeness.
theory_units.applies_when: When building intimacy or tension in a scene, starting from a less intimate perspective and progressively moving closer.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows the viewer to slowly become accustomed to the increasing level of intimacy, making subsequent close-ups more impactful and earned.
theory_units.caution: Moving in too quickly might feel abrupt, overly intimate, or reveal too much emotion prematurely for the stage of the action.

theory_units.title: Increasing Intimacy and Graphic Contrast with Closer Shots
theory_units.summary: After establishing emotional distance in a preceding shot, moving into a closer shot can involve the viewer more intimately and provide graphic contrast through the change in shot size.
theory_units.applies_when: When transitioning from a more distant or neutral perspective to a more personal, intense, or revealing moment within a sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightens viewer involvement and creates visual dynamism through the noticeable change in shot scale and proximity.

theory_units.title: Open Framing for Shared Psychological Point of View
